---
title: "Field Goals, Extra Points, and the Punting Game"
subtitle: "How a 1.3-second operation turns a drive into three points, why the extra point stopped being automatic, and what eleven men are really doing on fourth down when the punter jogs out."
description: "Field-goal geometry and range (kicker, wind, cold, altitude, roofs) with nflverse charts of accuracy across eras and conditions; the snap-hold-kick operation, protection rules and block units; the 2015 extra-point change and the two-point tries it produced; punt formations (tight, spread and shield), gunners and vices; directional, coffin-corner, rugby and pooch punts; net punting average and where punts finish; return walls, punt blocks and punt safe; the rules of the kicked ball (fair catch, touchback, muff, first touching, kick-catch interference, out of bounds); and why fakes are rare."
glossary:
  "Field goal range": "The yard line beyond which a coach believes his kicker, in today's conditions, makes a field goal often enough that kicking beats going for it or punting. Add 18 to the line of scrimmage for the kick's length; in the NFL range usually begins somewhere around the opponent's 35 to 40."
  "Snap-hold-kick": "The three-man field-goal and extra-point operation: the long snapper fires the ball about seven or eight yards back, the holder catches it and spots it on its point with the laces turned away, and the kicker strikes it, all in about 1.3 seconds from snap to kick (the 'operation time')."
  "Shield punt": {def: "The family of modern punt formations: two gunners split wide, a line of interior blockers, and a 'shield' of blockers a few yards in front of the punter that walls off rushers before they reach the spot of the kick. In the NFL the base version is usually called the spread punt, with two wings a yard behind the line and a personal protector about six yards deep forming the shield; the college version puts three blockers side by side.", aliases: ["Spread punt"]}
  "Vice": {def: "A punt-return player assigned to block a gunner at the line and run with him, usually two to a gunner, to slow the punt team's fastest coverage players. Coaches often spell it 'vise' and, strictly, use it for the two-man bracket, calling a lone blocker on a gunner a 'jammer'.", aliases: ["Jammer"]}
  "Fair catch": "A catch of a punt or kickoff by a returner who waves one fully extended arm above his helmet while the ball is in the air. He may not be hit, the ball is dead where he catches it, and he may not run with it."
  "Coffin-corner punt": "A punt aimed to go out of bounds just short of the goal line, near the corner of the field, so the receiving team must start its drive deep in its own territory without a chance to return the kick."
  "Touchback": "A ball declared dead in or behind a team's own end zone that the opponent kicked or carried there, with the defending team taking over at a fixed yard line instead of risking a safety. After a punt or a missed field goal from inside the 20, the ball goes to the 20; after a kickoff, see the kickoff chapter."
  "Net punting average": "Punting distance after subtracting return yards and 20 yards for every touchback, divided by the number of punts: the field position a punt actually gained, as opposed to how far it flew (gross average)."
  "Fake punt / fake field goal": "A play in which the kicking team lines up to punt or kick but runs or passes instead, usually with the punter, holder or personal protector handling the ball, to keep possession on fourth down or score."
  "Return wall": {def: "A punt return in which most of the return team peels back to one sideline and forms a line of blockers parallel to it, about five yards apart, and the returner runs behind that wall.", aliases: ["Wall return"]}
  "Punt block": "A return-team call that sends extra rushers, often overloading one side, to block the punt instead of returning it; rushers aim at a spot about a yard in front of the punter where the ball leaves his foot, not at the punter himself."
  "Punt safe": "A return-team call for when a fake is likely: the defense keeps (or sends on) its regular defenders, covers every eligible receiver and the likely ball carriers, and gives up most of the return to make sure the kicking team doesn't keep the ball."
  "Rugby punt": "A punt kicked on the run after the punter rolls out toward one side, usually as a low, end-over-end kick that bounces and rolls; it buys time against the rush, makes the ball hard to field, and can turn into a run if the edge is open."
  "Pooch punt": "A deliberately short, high punt from near midfield or closer, aimed to land inside the opponent's 10-yard line without bouncing into the end zone."
  "Muff": "Touching a loose ball, such as a punt, without gaining possession of it. A punt muffed by the receiving team can be recovered by the kicking team, which keeps the ball but may not advance it."
  "First touching": "A kicking-team player touching a punt beyond the line of scrimmage before any receiving player has touched it. It is a violation, not a foul: the ball stays live, and the receiving team may take the ball at the spot of first touching or at the end of the play, whichever it prefers."
  "Kick-catch interference": "A kicking-team player getting in the way of, or touching, a receiver who is trying to catch a punt or kickoff in the air, whether or not he signaled for a fair catch. The penalty is 15 yards from the spot of the foul."
  "Personal protector": "The punt team's last blocker and on-field leader, standing about five to seven yards behind the line: he calls the protection, blocks any rusher who gets through, and is a common ball carrier on fake punts."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (data and drawing helpers for this chapter)"
#| output: false
import logging
import os
import re
import shutil

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import polars as pl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch, Patch, Rectangle
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
from IPython.display import HTML, Markdown, display

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, style, draw_marker, frame_strip, animate
from gridiron.field import FIELD_WIDTH, MIDDLE
from gridiron.data import nfl

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
OC, DC = style.OFFENSE_DARK, style.DEFENSE_DARK
GREEN = "#0f7a55"          # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]   # rings on a player to watch


# --- markers, labels and arrows on a drawn field ------------------------------------------------
def O(key, pos, d, w, label=""):
    """A kicking-team (blue) player at (d, w): d = yards downfield of the line, w = yards to its right."""
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=""):
    """A receiving-team (orange) player."""
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def P_(fld, p, d, w):
    """(d, w) in the kicking team's frame -> plot coordinates on this drawn field."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    return float(x), float(y)


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fs=6.6, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = P_(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fs, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9, fontweight=weight,
                linespacing=1.1, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def lead(fld, p, frm, to, color=style.MUTED):
    """A thin leader line from a label at `frm` to a player at `to`."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P_(fld, p, *frm), P_(fld, p, *to)
    fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=0.7, zorder=7.5)


def ball_arrow(fld, p, frm, to, rad=0.0, lw=1.2, color=style.BALL):
    """The ball's flight (snap or kick) as a dashed brown arrow."""
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(P_(fld, p, *frm), P_(fld, p, *to), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9,
                                     color=color, lw=lw, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=7,
                                     connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}"))


def ball_at(fld, p, d, w):
    x, y = P_(fld, p, d, w)
    draw_marker(fld.ax, x, y, "ball", "", fld.pts_per_yard())


def no_numbers(fld):
    """Remove the painted yard numbers (they compete with labels on zoomed diagrams)."""
    for t in list(fld.ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit():
            t.remove()


def shade(fld, p, d0, d1, w0, w1, color, alpha=0.10):
    """A shaded rectangle between depths d0..d1 and widths w0..w1."""
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = P_(fld, p, d0, w0), P_(fld, p, d1, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(xa, xb), min(ya, yb)), abs(xb - xa), abs(yb - ya), fc=color,
                               alpha=alpha, ec="none", zorder=1))


# --- animations: gridiron tracking, with the ball's flight replaced by the kick's --------------
def with_ball(play, ball_fn, t_after=0.6):
    """Simulated tracking (BDB columns) for a kicking play. gridiron's ball model follows a QB;
    here `ball_fn(t)` gives the ball's (d, w): snap, hold or catch, then the kick."""
    df = play.to_tracking(t_after=t_after)
    m = df.side == "ball"
    dw = np.array([ball_fn(t) for t in df.loc[m, "time"]])
    x, y = play.to_abs(dw[:, 0], dw[:, 1])
    df.loc[m, "x"], df.loc[m, "y"] = x, y
    return df


def lerp(a, b, f):
    f = min(max(f, 0.0), 1.0)
    return (a[0] + (b[0] - a[0]) * f, a[1] + (b[1] - a[1]) * f)


def sxy(play, d, w):
    """(d, w) -> plot coordinates inside a gridiron frame strip (vertical view)."""
    x, y = play.to_abs(d, w)
    return float(FIELD_WIDTH - y), float(x)


def strip_text(ax, play, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fs=6.0):
    x, y = sxy(play, d, w)
    ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fs, color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=12, linespacing=1.05,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def show_strip(df, times, annotate=None, title=None, lateral_pad=4.0):
    """HTML: a scrubbable video of the simulated tracking. PDF: a frame strip at `times`."""
    if PDF:
        fig = frame_strip(df, times=times, title=title, lateral_pad=lateral_pad)
        for ax in fig.axes:          # painted yard numbers land outside the cropped panels; drop them
            for t in list(ax.texts):
                if t.get_text().isdigit():
                    t.remove()
        fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.6)
        if annotate:
            annotate(fig.axes[:len(times)])
        plt.show()
        return
    anim = animate(df, title=title)
    if shutil.which("ffmpeg"):
        html = anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
    else:
        html = anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once")
    plt.close(anim._fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def md_table(rows, header, align):
    lines = ["| " + " | ".join(header) + " |", "|" + "|".join(align) + "|"]
    lines += ["| " + " | ".join(map(str, r)) + " |" for r in rows]
    return Markdown("\n".join(lines))


def pct(v, d=0):
    return f"{100 * v:.{d}f}%"
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (load every kicking play since 1999 from nflverse)"
#| output: false
SEASONS = range(1999, 2026)   # nflverse play-by-play starts in 1999; 2025 is the last completed season
KEEP = ["season", "season_type", "week", "game_id", "posteam", "home_team", "play_type", "desc",
        "yardline_100", "down", "ydstogo", "kick_distance", "field_goal_result", "extra_point_result",
        "two_point_conv_result", "two_point_attempt", "roof", "temp", "wind", "weather",
        "kicker_player_name", "touchback", "punt_inside_twenty", "punt_out_of_bounds", "punt_downed",
        "punt_fair_catch", "return_yards", "punt_blocked", "first_down"]


def kicking_plays():
    """Field goals, extra points, two-point tries, punts, fourth-down runs and passes, and runs/passes
    from kick formations."""
    out = []
    for s in SEASONS:
        df = nfl().load_pbp([s])
        df = df.filter(pl.col("play_type").is_in(["field_goal", "punt", "extra_point"])
                       | (pl.col("two_point_attempt") == 1)
                       | ((pl.col("down") == 4) & pl.col("play_type").is_in(["run", "pass"]))
                       | pl.col("desc").str.contains("Punt formation|Field Goal formation"))
        out.append(df.select([c for c in KEEP if c in df.columns]).to_pandas())
    return pd.concat(out, ignore_index=True)


K = kicking_plays()
reg = K[K.season_type == "REG"]
S = {}                        # numbers quoted in the text

# --- field goals ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
fg = reg[reg.play_type == "field_goal"].copy()
fg["made"] = fg.field_goal_result.eq("made")
S["fg18"] = pct(((fg.kick_distance - fg.yardline_100) == 18).mean())
S["fg_blk"] = pct((fg[fg.season.between(2021, 2025)].field_goal_result == "blocked").mean(), 1)

ERA_EDGES, ERA_LABS = [1998, 2005, 2012, 2019, 2025], ["1999–2005", "2006–2012", "2013–2019", "2020–2025"]
D_EDGES = [17, 24, 29, 34, 39, 44, 49, 54, 59, 80]
D_LABS = ["18–24", "25–29", "30–34", "35–39", "40–44", "45–49", "50–54", "55–59", "60+"]
fg["era"] = pd.cut(fg.season, ERA_EDGES, labels=ERA_LABS)
fg["dbin"] = pd.cut(fg.kick_distance, D_EDGES, labels=D_LABS)
era_tab = fg.groupby(["era", "dbin"], observed=True).made.agg(["mean", "size"]).reset_index()
f50 = fg[fg.kick_distance >= 50]
S["m50_e1"] = pct(f50[f50.era == ERA_LABS[0]].made.mean())
S["m50_e4"] = pct(f50[f50.era == ERA_LABS[3]].made.mean())
share50 = fg.groupby("era", observed=True).kick_distance.apply(lambda x: (x >= 50).mean())
S["sh50_e1"], S["sh50_e4"] = pct(share50.iloc[0]), pct(share50.iloc[3])
S["att50_99"] = f"{(fg[fg.season == 1999].kick_distance >= 50).sum()}"
S["att50_25"] = f"{(fg[fg.season == 2025].kick_distance >= 50).sum()}"
m60 = fg[fg.made & (fg.kick_distance >= 60)].groupby("season").size()
S["m60_25"] = f"{m60.get(2025, 0)}"
S["m60_1924"] = f"{m60.loc[2019:2024].mean():.0f}"
S["m55_25"] = f"{(fg[fg.made & (fg.kick_distance >= 55)].season == 2025).sum()}"
S["m55_1621"] = f"{fg[fg.made & (fg.kick_distance >= 55) & fg.season.between(2016, 2021)].groupby('season').size().mean():.0f}"


# --- weather: roof, temperature and wind for 2010-2025 kicks ------------------------------------
def from_weather(s, pat):
    m = re.search(pat, s) if isinstance(s, str) else None
    return float(m.group(1)) if m else np.nan


wx = fg[fg.season.between(2010, 2025)].copy()
wx["indoor"] = wx.roof.isin(["dome", "closed"])
wx["tempF"] = wx.temp.fillna(wx.weather.map(lambda s: from_weather(s, r"Temp:\s*(-?\d+)")))
wx["windmph"] = wx.wind.fillna(wx.weather.map(lambda s: from_weather(s, r"Wind:\s*[A-Za-z]*\s*(\d+)\s*mph")))
W_EDGES, W_LABS = [17, 29, 39, 49, 54, 80], ["18–29", "30–39", "40–49", "50–54", "55+"]
wx["wbin"] = pd.cut(wx.kick_distance, W_EDGES, labels=W_LABS)
out = wx[~wx.indoor]
cold, warm = out[out.tempF < 40], out[out.tempF >= 60]
GROUPS = {"Indoors (dome or closed roof)": wx[wx.indoor], "Outdoors": out,
          "Outdoors, below 40°F": cold, "Outdoors, 60°F or warmer": warm}
wx_tab = {k: g.groupby("wbin", observed=True).made.agg(["mean", "size"]) for k, g in GROUPS.items()}
for key, g in [("in", wx[wx.indoor]), ("out", out), ("cold", cold), ("warm", warm)]:
    S[f"sh50_{key}"] = pct((g.kick_distance >= 50).mean())
    S[f"m50_{key}"] = pct(g[g.kick_distance >= 50].made.mean())
calm, windy = out[out.windmph <= 5], out[out.windmph >= 11]
S["m5054_calm"] = pct(calm[calm.kick_distance.between(50, 54)].made.mean())
S["m5054_windy"] = pct(windy[windy.kick_distance.between(50, 54)].made.mean())
S["sh50_calm"], S["sh50_windy"] = pct((calm.kick_distance >= 50).mean()), pct((windy.kick_distance >= 50).mean())
den = wx.home_team.eq("DEN")
S["den55"] = pct((wx[den].kick_distance >= 55).mean())
S["oth55"] = pct((wx[~den].kick_distance >= 55).mean())
c55 = cold[cold.kick_distance.between(55, 59)]
w55 = warm[warm.kick_distance.between(55, 59)]
S["c55"], S["w55"], S["c55n"] = pct(c55.made.mean()), pct(w55.made.mean()), f"{len(c55)}"
S["c50"] = pct(cold[cold.kick_distance.between(50, 54)].made.mean())
S["c55p"], S["w55p"] = pct(cold[cold.kick_distance >= 55].made.mean()), pct(warm[warm.kick_distance >= 55].made.mean())
S["c55pn"] = f"{(cold.kick_distance >= 55).sum()}"

# --- kickers in the film room ----------------------------------------------------------------------
tk = fg[fg.kicker_player_name.eq("J.Tucker")]
S["tucker_pct"], S["tucker_att"] = pct(tk.made.mean(), 1), f"{len(tk)}"
S["tucker24"] = f"{tk[tk.season == 2024].made.sum()} of {(tk.season == 2024).sum()}"
ab = fg[fg.kicker_player_name.eq("B.Aubrey")]
S["aub50_24"] = f"{(ab[(ab.season == 2024)].made & (ab[ab.season == 2024].kick_distance >= 50)).sum()}"
S["aub50att_24"] = f"{(ab[ab.season == 2024].kick_distance >= 50).sum()}"
S["aub60"] = f"{(ab.made & (ab.kick_distance >= 60)).sum()}"
S["aub_sh50"] = pct((ab.kick_distance >= 50).mean())
S["lg_sh50_2325"] = pct((fg[fg.season.between(2023, 2025)].kick_distance >= 50).mean())
lt = fg[fg.kicker_player_name.eq("C.Little") & (fg.season == 2025)]
S["little25"] = f"{lt.made.sum()} of {len(lt)}"

# --- the try: extra points and two-point conversions ----------------------------------------
xp = reg[reg.play_type == "extra_point"]
tp = reg[(reg.two_point_attempt == 1) & reg.two_point_conv_result.notna()]
try_tab = pd.DataFrame({
    "xp_att": xp.groupby("season").size(),
    "xp_pct": xp.groupby("season").extra_point_result.apply(lambda x: (x == "good").mean()),
    "tp_att": tp.groupby("season").size(),
    "tp_pct": tp.groupby("season").two_point_conv_result.apply(lambda x: (x == "success").mean())})
try_tab["tp_share"] = try_tab.tp_att / (try_tab.tp_att + try_tab.xp_att)
S["xp14"], S["xp15"] = pct(try_tab.xp_pct[2014], 1), pct(try_tab.xp_pct[2015], 1)
S["xp_2125"] = pct(try_tab.xp_pct.loc[2021:2025].mean(), 1)
S["tp14"], S["tp15"] = f"{try_tab.tp_att[2014]}", f"{try_tab.tp_att[2015]}"
S["tp_1014"] = f"{try_tab.tp_att.loc[2010:2014].mean():.0f}"
S["tp_2125"] = f"{try_tab.tp_att.loc[2021:2025].mean():.0f}"
S["tp_pct_1525"] = pct(tp[tp.season >= 2015].two_point_conv_result.eq("success").mean())
S["tp_val"] = f"{2 * tp[tp.season >= 2015].two_point_conv_result.eq('success').mean():.2f}"
S["xp_val"] = f"{xp[xp.season >= 2015].extra_point_result.eq('good').mean():.2f}"
tp_team = tp[tp.season >= 2015].groupby("posteam").size().sort_values(ascending=False)
TEAM = {"PHI": "Philadelphia", "JAX": "Jacksonville", "TB": "Tampa Bay", "PIT": "Pittsburgh", "CLE": "Cleveland",
        "WAS": "Washington"}
S["tp_top"] = f"{TEAM.get(tp_team.index[0], tp_team.index[0])}, with {tp_team.iloc[0]} tries"
xpb = xp.groupby("season").extra_point_result.apply(lambda x: (x == "blocked").sum())
S["xpblk_1014"], S["xpblk_1525"] = f"{xpb.loc[2010:2014].mean():.0f}", f"{xpb.loc[2015:2025].mean():.0f}"
S["xpblk_lo"], S["xpblk_hi"] = f"{xpb.loc[2015:2025].min()}", f"{xpb.loc[2015:2025].max()}"
S["tp23"], S["tp24"] = pct(try_tab.tp_pct[2023]), pct(try_tab.tp_pct[2024])
_p, _n = try_tab.tp_pct.loc[2015:2025].mean(), try_tab.tp_att.loc[2021:2025].mean()
S["tp_moe"] = f"{200 * np.sqrt(_p * (1 - _p) / _n):.0f}"      # two standard errors, in points

# --- punts -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
pu = reg[reg.play_type == "punt"].copy()
pu["ret"] = pu.return_yards.fillna(0)
pu["net"] = pu.kick_distance.fillna(0) - pu.ret - 20 * pu.touchback
pu["fin"] = pu.yardline_100 - pu.kick_distance          # receiving team's yard line where the kick ended
trend = pu.groupby("season").agg(gross=("kick_distance", "mean"), net=("net", "mean"),
                                 fc=("punt_fair_catch", "mean"), n=("net", "size"))
S["gross99"], S["net99"] = f"{trend.gross[1999]:.1f}", f"{trend.net[1999]:.1f}"
S["gross25"], S["net25"] = f"{trend.gross[2025]:.1f}", f"{trend.net[2025]:.1f}"
S["ret_9903"] = f"{(trend.gross - trend.net).loc[1999:2003].mean():.1f}"
S["ret_2125"] = f"{(trend.gross - trend.net).loc[2021:2025].mean():.1f}"
S["fc99"], S["fc25"] = pct(trend.fc.loc[1999:2003].mean()), pct(trend.fc.loc[2021:2025].mean())
S["punts99"], S["punts25"] = f"{trend.n[1999]:,}", f"{trend.n[2025]:,}"
recent = pu[pu.season.between(2021, 2025) & (pu.punt_blocked == 0)]
mid = recent[recent.yardline_100.between(40, 50)]
S["mid_tb"] = pct(mid.touchback.mean())
S["mid_in10"] = pct(((mid.fin <= 10) & (mid.fin > 0)).mean())
S["mid_n"] = f"{len(mid):,}"
S["oob10"] = pct(((recent.punt_out_of_bounds == 1) & recent.fin.between(1, 10)).mean(), 1)
S["down10"] = pct(((recent.punt_downed == 1) & recent.fin.between(1, 10)).mean(), 1)
deep = recent[recent.yardline_100 >= 80]
S["deep_fin"] = f"{deep.fin.mean():.0f}"
S["blk_punts"] = f"{pu[pu.season.between(2021, 2025)].punt_blocked.sum() / 5:.0f}"
muff = recent.desc.str.contains("MUFFS", na=False)
S["muffs"] = f"{muff.sum() / 5:.0f}"

# --- fakes: runs and passes the play-by-play tags as coming from a kicking formation ----------------
scrim = reg[reg.play_type.isin(["run", "pass"]) & reg.season.between(2016, 2025)
            & ~reg.desc.str.contains("Aborted", na=False)]
fp = scrim[scrim.desc.str.contains("Punt formation", na=False)]
ff = scrim[scrim.desc.str.contains("Field Goal formation", na=False)]
punts_1625 = (pu.season.between(2016, 2025)).sum()
S["fp_yr"] = f"{len(fp) / 10:.0f}"
S["fp_conv"] = pct(fp.first_down.mean())
S["fp_rate"] = pct(len(fp) / (len(fp) + punts_1625), 1)
S["ff_yr"] = f"{len(ff) / 10:.0f}"
go4 = reg[(reg.down == 4) & reg.play_type.isin(["run", "pass"]) & reg.season.between(2016, 2025)
          & ~reg.desc.str.contains("formation\\)", na=False, regex=True)]
S["c4_6"] = pct(go4[go4.ydstogo == 6].first_down.mean())
S["ff_9905"] = f"{len(reg[reg.play_type.isin(['run', 'pass']) & reg.season.between(1999, 2005) & reg.desc.str.contains('Field Goal formation', na=False)]) / 7:.0f}"
```

Fourth-and-7 at the opponent's 36, late in the third quarter, down by four. The broadcast cuts to
the sideline, where the kicker has been swinging his leg into a practice net for two minutes. The
graphic says **54-yard attempt**. The head coach looks up at the flags on top of the goal posts,
which are snapping straight back toward the line of scrimmage (a wind in the kicker's face), says
something into his headset, and sends out... the punter. The punter, from barely 50 yards away, then
tries to kick the ball *short*: high, soft, aimed at the 8. Two of his teammates sprint past everyone
the instant the ball is snapped. The returner stands under it, waves one arm over his head, catches
it at the 9, and nobody lays a finger on him. Why wasn't 54 yards in range today, when the same
kicker made a 56-yarder last month? Why would anyone want a short punt? And what was that wave? This
chapter is about the plays that start with a long snap: the field goal, the extra point and the
punt. They are about one snap in six, they decide a large share of close games, and they are full
of rules most viewers have never had explained.

**You'll be able to…**

- Turn any line of scrimmage into a field-goal distance in your head, and judge whether it is in
  range *for this kicker, today*: roof or open sky, cold, wind, altitude.
- Watch a field goal as a 1.3-second operation (snap, hold, kick) behind a wall that must not give
  ground, and spot how a block unit (the defense's kick-blocking team) attacks it.
- Explain why the extra point moved back in 2015 and what that did to two-point tries.
- Read an NFL punt formation: name the gunners, the vices, the wings and personal protector who form
  the shield, and say whether the return team is setting up a return, a block or a "safe" look.
- Call the rules of a kicked ball as it happens: fair catch, touchback, downing, out of bounds,
  muff versus fumble, first touching and kick-catch interference.
- Explain why fakes succeed more often than not and are still rare.

## The third phase in one minute

Every football team is really three teams. The offense and defense get the airtime; the third,
**special teams**, takes the field for the kicking plays: kickoffs, punts, field goals and extra
points. Those were 17.5% of NFL plays in 2025, about one snap in six (the count is in
[What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)), and they are run by
their own coach, the
[special teams coordinator](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd). You met the
specialists (kicker, punter, long snapper, holder, returner and gunners) in
[The Twenty-Two](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd). This chapter puts them to work.

Two kinds of kicks are in this chapter. Both are **scrimmage kicks**: they start with a snap from
the line of scrimmage, like any offensive play, and the offense chooses them, usually on fourth
down. The field goal tries to score; the punt gives the ball away on purpose in exchange for field
position. (The kickoff, a *free* kick from a tee that starts each half and follows every score, is
a different animal with its own fast-changing rules; it has its own chapter,
[Kickoffs, Returns, and the Dynamic Kickoff](09-02-kickoffs-and-returns.qmd).)

Why should a viewer who cares about schemes care about kicking? Because the kicking game sets the
price of everything else. How far out a kicker can be trusted decides where a fourth down becomes
a field-goal try instead of a gamble. How far a punter can pin the opponent decides how much a
failed fourth-down try costs. Every fourth-down decision you will learn to judge in
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)
starts with the numbers in this chapter.

## Field goals: from the line of scrimmage to the crossbar

You already know the basic deal from
[The Game in Fifteen Minutes](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd): a
[field goal](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd) is three points for kicking
the ball, held on the ground, through the goal posts, from anywhere on the field, on any down. Here
we take it apart, starting with the arithmetic every broadcast does for you.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fg-geometry
#| fig-cap: "Where a field goal's length comes from, kicking team moving left to right from the opponent's 30. The ball is snapped about 8 yards back to the holder (the curved dashed snap), who spots it there; the kick (solid line) starts from that spot, and the goal posts stand on the end line, 10 yards behind the goal line. So the kick is the yard line plus 18: 30 + 8 + 10 = 48 yards. The uprights are 18 feet 6 inches apart, exactly the width between the NFL's hash marks, so even a kick from a hash meets the posts at only a slight angle."
def fg_geometry(ax, los_yd, title=None, show_dims=True, extra=None, lat=(-14.5, 14.5), range_line=None):
    """A field goal from the opponent's `los_yd`, drawn horizontally (kicking left to right).
    The snap is a curved dashed arrow and the kick a solid one, so the two never read as one line.
    `range_line`: an opponent's yard line to mark as the kicker's range line (dashed)."""
    los_x = 110 - los_yd
    team = [O("LS", "C", -0.7, 0.0, "LS"), O("HOLD", "P", -8.0, 1.1, "Ho"), O("K", "K", -10.4, -2.1, "K")]
    p = Play(team, [], los=los_x, to_go=None)
    fld = p.draw(orient="horizontal", window=(-14.0, 120 - los_x), lateral=lat, title=False, ax=ax)
    ax = fld.ax
    no_numbers(fld)
    for xx in range(int(np.ceil((fld.x0 + 2.5) / 10) * 10), 111, 10):
        lab = "goal line" if xx == 110 else (f"{110 - xx}" if xx > 60 else f"{xx - 10}")
        if xx == 110 - los_yd or (range_line is not None and abs(xx - (110 - range_line)) < 4):
            continue
        nx, ny = fld.xy(xx, MIDDLE + lat[1] - 1.8)
        ax.text(float(nx), float(ny), lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.MUTED,
                fontweight="bold", zorder=3)
    ball_at(fld, p, -8.0, 0.0)
    ball_arrow(fld, p, (0.0, 0.0), (-7.5, -0.3), rad=0.45, lw=1.0)      # the snap, bowed to one side
    if range_line is not None:
        rx = 110 - range_line
        (ax0, ay0), (ax1, ay1) = fld.xy(rx, MIDDLE + lat[0] + 1.0), fld.xy(rx, MIDDLE + lat[1] - 3.2)
        ax.plot([float(ax0), float(ax1)], [float(ay0), float(ay1)], color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=1.4,
                ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=4)
    # goal posts on the end line (BDB x = 120): crossbar 18'6" wide, centred
    half = 18.5 / 3 / 2
    (gx0, gy0), (gx1, gy1) = fld.xy(119.7, MIDDLE - half), fld.xy(119.7, MIDDLE + half)
    ax.plot([gx0, gx1], [gy0, gy1], color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=3.2, solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=6)
    for yy in (MIDDLE - half, MIDDLE + half):
        (ux, uy), _ = fld.xy(119.7, yy), None
        ax.plot([ux], [uy], marker="o", ms=4, color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, zorder=6)
    # the kick's path, spot to the middle of the crossbar: solid, so it can't be mistaken for the snap
    kx, ky = fld.xy(los_x - 7.4, MIDDLE)
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(kx), float(ky)), (float(gx0 + gx1) / 2 - 0.4, float(gy0 + gy1) / 2),
                                 arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10, color=style.BALL, lw=1.6, zorder=5))
    if show_dims:
        yd = MIDDLE - 11.0   # dimension line a little toward the offense's right
        segs = [(los_x - 8.0, los_x, "8 yd\n(snap)"), (los_x, 110.0, f"{los_yd} yd\n(line to goal line)"),
                (110.0, 120.0, "10 yd\n(end zone)")]
        for a, b, lab in segs:
            (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = fld.xy(a, yd), fld.xy(b, yd)
            ax.annotate("", xy=(float(xb), float(yb)), xytext=(float(xa), float(ya)),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0), zorder=6)
            ax.text((float(xa) + float(xb)) / 2, float(ya) - 1.2, lab, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.6,
                    color=style.INK_2, zorder=7, linespacing=1.05)
    return fld, p


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.3))
fld, p = fg_geometry(ax, 30)
say(fld, p, 0.0, 3.3, "line of\nscrimmage\n(opp. 30)", color=OC, fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, -8.0, 4.4, "spot of\nthe kick", color=OC, fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, -3.8, -3.0, "snap", color=style.BALL, fs=6.2)
say(fld, p, 9.0, 1.6, "kick", color=style.BALL, fs=6.2)
gx, gy = fld.xy(116.4, MIDDLE + 6.4)
ax.text(float(gx), float(gy) - 1.5, "goal posts\non the\nend line", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.4,
        color=style.INK_2, zorder=9, linespacing=1.05)
tx, ty = fld.xy(96.0, MIDDLE + 6.0)
ax.text(float(tx), float(ty), "30 + 8 + 10 = a 48-yard kick", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5,
        color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", zorder=9,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))
plt.show()
```

The rule of thumb is **add 18**: from the opponent's 30, a 48-yarder; from the 36, a 54-yarder.
The 18 is the 10-yard end zone (the posts have stood at the back of it, on the end line, since
1974) plus the distance between the line of scrimmage and the spot where the holder sets the ball:
about 7 to 8 yards on the field, and 8 by the scorers' convention, which is where "add 18" comes
from. In nflverse play-by-play since 1999, `{python} S["fg18"]` of all field-goal attempts are
recorded at exactly the line of scrimmage plus 18.[^fg18] That share reflects the scorers' rule of
thumb more than a tape measure: nobody measures where the holder's finger actually was. College
announcers often say "add 17," because many college holders kneel a yard closer.

Why does the holder kneel so far back? Because of the rushers. A kicked ball rises steeply, but it
needs a few yards of travel to climb above the outstretched hands of the defenders at the line.
Move the spot closer and the ball is still low when it crosses the line, so it is easier to block.
Move it farther back and the ball clears the line easily, but now the snap takes longer, the kick is
longer and less accurate, and edge rushers have more time to get around the end to the spot. Seven
to eight yards is where a century of trial and error settled.

The goal itself is a crossbar 10 feet off the ground and 18 feet 6 inches wide, with uprights
reaching 35 feet above it.[^posts] That width is no accident of design: the NFL's hash marks are
18 feet 6 inches apart too, so a kick from either hash is lined up directly with one upright and
needs only a mild angle. In college, where the hashes are much wider, kickers face real angles from
the hash, which is why college teams sometimes waste a down running the ball to the middle of the
field before a kick. In the NFL the hash matters much less, though many kickers still have a side
they prefer.

### What "field goal range" means

[**Field goal range**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-field-goal-range) is the yard line
beyond which a coach believes his kicker makes the kick often enough, today, that kicking beats the
alternatives. Notice the three parts of that definition. It is *a coach's belief*, not a fact
painted on the field. It depends on *today*: the wind, the cold, the roof. And it is *relative to
the alternatives*: going for it on fourth down, or punting. A 55-yard try that goes in six times in
ten might be a great call on fourth-and-9 and a poor one on fourth-and-1.

Coaches don't guess at the first part. Before every game, kickers warm up from progressively
longer distances toward *both* end zones and tell the special teams coordinator their lines: "the
35 going this way, the 31 going the other way, into the wind." Those yard lines go on the call sheet
next to the fourth-down plan, and they are why the coach in the opening scene looked at the flags.

The cost of a miss is the other half. A missed field goal isn't like a punt. The other team takes
over at the spot of the kick, where the holder put the ball down, or at its own 20 if the kick came
from inside the 20.[^missedfg] So a missed 54-yarder from the opponent's 36 hands the other team the
ball at its own 44: you didn't score, *and* you gave them a short field. A punt from the same spot
would have pinned them somewhere near their 10. Range is the yard line where those two prices
balance. (How often is "often enough"? That depends on the score, the clock and the distance to go,
and the arithmetic is built in
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).)

One more way a miss can hurt. A field-goal try that falls short in the field of play or the end zone
is a live ball, and once a defender touches it the special missed-kick rule no longer applies: it is
treated like a punt, and he may catch it and run it back.[^fgreturn] That is why defenses station a
returner under the crossbar on very long tries. On November 4, 2007, at Minnesota, San Diego's
Antonio Cromartie caught a missed 57-yarder nine yards deep in his own end zone and returned it
109 yards for a touchdown, at the time the longest play in league history.[^cromartie]

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game the kicker's range is a meter: aim, press, and the leg is exactly as strong on a
frozen December night in Buffalo as indoors in September. Real range moves from week to week and
from one end of the field to the other in the same game. The NFL head coach doesn't have a meter;
he has a pregame report from his kicker, a forecast, the flags on the uprights, and a fourth-down
chart from his analytics staff. Watch the end of warmups on a windy day and you'll see kickers
deliberately trying long kicks into the wind to find out where the line is.
:::

### Kickers keep getting better

```{python}
#| label: fig-fg-eras
#| fig-cap: "How often NFL field goals are made, by distance, in four eras (regular seasons). Every era is near-perfect from inside 30 yards; the eras separate at distance. A 50–54-yard kick that was a coin flip around the turn of the century is now made about three times in four, and kicks of 55–59 yards are better today than 45–49-yard kicks were in 1999–2005. Points are shown only where an era has at least 25 attempts in that distance band. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
cols = [style.SERIES[3], style.SERIES[2], style.SERIES[1], style.SERIES[0]]
for era, col in zip(ERA_LABS, cols):
    t = era_tab[(era_tab.era == era) & (era_tab["size"] >= 25)]
    xs = [D_LABS.index(b) for b in t.dbin]
    ax.plot(xs, t["mean"] * 100, color=col, marker="o", ms=4, lw=2, label=era)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(D_LABS)), D_LABS)
ax.set_xlabel("kick distance (yards)")
ax.set_ylabel("made (%)")
ax.set_ylim(15, 102)
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8, title="seasons", title_fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

The chart is one of the clearest skill trends in the sport.[^eras] Kicks from 50 yards and beyond
were made `{python} S["m50_e1"]` of the time in 1999–2005 and `{python} S["m50_e4"]` in 2020–2025.
Coaches noticed: kicks of 50-plus were `{python} S["sh50_e1"]` of all attempts in the first era and
`{python} S["sh50_e4"]` in the latest (`{python} S["att50_99"]` such attempts in 1999,
`{python} S["att50_25"]` in 2025). From 1999 through 2005, seven full seasons, no NFL kicker made a
field goal of 60 yards or more; in 2025 alone kickers made `{python} S["m60_25"]`.

Why? Several things at once, and nobody can cleanly split the credit:

- **Specialization.** Kickers used to be position players who also kicked. The last of the
  straight-on, toe-first kickers left the NFL in the 1980s, replaced by soccer-style kickers who swing
  into the ball with the instep, a technique Hungarian-born Pete Gogolak brought to pro football
  with the Buffalo Bills of the AFL (the American Football League, the NFL's 1960s rival, which
  merged with it in 1970) in 1964.[^gogolak] Today's kickers are year-round specialists, many
  with soccer backgrounds, private kicking coaches and video of every rep.
- **Competition for jobs.** There are only 32 jobs. A kicker who makes 80% gets cut for one who makes 88%,
  and the pool of candidates (college, other leagues, soccer) has grown.
- **The ball.** Through 2024 the special "K-balls" used for kicks were shipped to the officials and
  handed to each team only an hour before the game, to be prepared with towels and a brush. For
  2025 the league let teams receive their kicking balls before the season and break them in like
  quarterbacks' balls. Kickers had long complained that a ball fresh out of the box, not yet broken
  in, felt hard and dead off the foot. Long-range kicking jumped in 2025:
  `{python} S["m55_25"]` made kicks of 55-plus yards, against about `{python} S["m55_1621"]` a season
  from 2016 to 2021.[^kball]

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Kicks from 50 yards are a coin flip." That was true in 2000. It hasn't been true for a decade, and
many fans (and some broadcasters) still talk as if it were. The practical effect is that **field-goal
range has moved out about five yards in a generation**, from roughly the opponent's 32 to roughly
the 37–40 for a good kicker indoors. Every one of those yards changes fourth-down math.
:::

### Wind, cold, altitude and roofs

The ball doesn't know the score, but it knows the air. Four conditions move range:

- **Wind** is the obvious one. A 15-mph wind in the kicker's face can take five or more yards off
  his range; at his back it adds them. Crosswinds push the ball sideways, which is why kickers aim
  "off" the upright in a crosswind. That's why kickers study the flags on top of the uprights before
  every kick.
- **Cold** costs distance twice. Cold air is denser, so the ball meets more drag, and a cold ball is
  harder and less lively off the foot. Kickers talk about a cold ball feeling like a rock.
- **Altitude** gives distance back. Denver's stadium sits about a mile above sea level, where the
  air is roughly 15% thinner, so the ball carries farther. Coaches lean on it a little: in
  2010–2025, `{python} S["den55"]` of field-goal attempts in Denver were from 55 yards or more,
  against `{python} S["oth55"]` everywhere else.
- **Roofs** remove the first two. A dome is warm and still every week.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fg-weather
#| fig-cap: "The weather box: field-goal accuracy by distance, 2010–2025 regular seasons. Left: indoors (domes and closed roofs) against outdoors. Right: outdoor games below 40°F against outdoor games at 60°F or warmer. Kicks inside 40 yards hardly care; the gap opens with distance. And these gaps are smaller than the real effect of the weather, because coaches decline the hardest kicks: in cold and wind they punt or go for it instead, so the long kicks that are tried in bad conditions are the ones the coach liked. Points are shown only where a group has at least 25 attempts. Source: nflverse play-by-play (roof, temperature and wind as recorded for each game)."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.0), sharey=True)
pairs = [(("Indoors (dome or closed roof)", style.SERIES[0]), ("Outdoors", style.SERIES[1])),
         (("Outdoors, 60°F or warmer", style.SERIES[3]), ("Outdoors, below 40°F", style.SERIES[6]))]
for ax, pair in zip(axes, pairs):
    for name, col in pair:
        t = wx_tab[name]
        t = t[t["size"] >= 25]
        ax.plot([W_LABS.index(b) for b in t.index], t["mean"] * 100, color=col, marker="o", ms=4, lw=2,
                label=name)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(W_LABS)), W_LABS, fontsize=7.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("kick distance (yards)", fontsize=8)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=7)
axes[0].set_ylabel("made (%)")
axes[0].set_ylim(35, 102)
axes[0].set_title("Roof", fontsize=9.5)
axes[1].set_title("Temperature (outdoor games)", fontsize=9.5)
plt.show()
```

The weather box shows the effect, and it also shows the most important trap in sports data:
**selection bias**, which means the cases in your data were chosen by someone, so they aren't a fair
sample.[^weather] Four numbers make the point. From 55 yards and beyond, outdoor kickers made
`{python} S["c55p"]` of their tries in games colder than 40°F and `{python} S["w55p"]` in games at 60°F
or warmer. But kicks of 50-plus were only `{python} S["sh50_cold"]` of attempts in the cold, against
`{python} S["sh50_warm"]` in the warm.

Picture how that happens. On a warm, still afternoon a coach lets his kicker try a 55-yarder whenever
the drive stalls near the opponent's 37. On a freezing night he lets him try it only when everything
else is in his favor: the wind at his back, a big-legged kicker, the last seconds of a half with
nothing to lose. So the long kicks in the cold column are a hand-picked, easier-than-average set, and
they *still* miss more often. The true cost of a long kick in the cold is larger than the gap in the
chart. Wind works the same way, with a second blur: the data records the wind's speed but not its
direction, so a gale at the kicker's back counts the same as one in his face.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: the record kick and where it was kicked"}
The longest field goals in NFL history read like a weather report. Tom Dempsey's 63-yarder for
New Orleans in 1970 stood as the record for 43 years; it was tied in Denver twice (Jason Elam in
1998, Sebastian Janikowski in 2011) and once at Green Bay (David Akers, 2012). Matt Prater broke it
with 64 yards in Denver in December 2013. Justin Tucker's 66 came indoors in Detroit in 2021, and
Cam Little's 68 came indoors in Las Vegas in November 2025.[^records] Thin air, then roofs: the
record has spent most of its modern life in places where the air helps.
:::

## The operation: snap, hold, kick

A field goal looks like one man's moment. It is really a three-man relay with a stopwatch on it.

[**Snap-hold-kick**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-snap-hold-kick) is the name for that relay,
and coaches time it from the snap to the moment the foot hits the ball, a number they call
**operation time**. The professional target is about **1.3 seconds**.[^optime] Here is what has to
happen inside it:

1. **The snap (roughly 0.4 seconds).** The long snapper, head down and looking backward between
   his legs, fires a tight spiral seven or eight yards to the holder's hands, ideally with the laces
   arriving in a predictable position.
2. **The hold (about half a second).** The holder catches it, puts the point on the ground on his
   mark, tilts it as his kicker likes and spins the laces to face the goal posts, because a foot
   that strikes the laces sends the ball off line.
3. **The kick.** The kicker has already started. He takes a small jab step as the snap leaves the
   snapper's hands and two strides at an angle, so his plant foot lands beside the ball just as it
   touches down, and swings through.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fg-operation
#| fig-cap: "The 1.3-second operation, simulated tracking in Big Data Bowl format (illustrative timing, not a real play). Snap: the field-goal unit and a ten-man block unit (the defense's kick-blocking team). 0.4 s: the snap reaches the holder (Ho). 0.9 s: the ball is down and the kicker (K) is on his second step; the interior rushers have been stopped at the line. 1.3 s: the kick is away, and the unblocked edge rusher on the overloaded side is still a couple of yards short of the spot where he could block it. Add a tenth of a second to the operation, a slow snap or a bobbled hold, and he gets there."
def fg_unit(split=1.4):
    pl_ = [O("LS", "C", -0.7, 0.0, "LS")]
    for k, w in [("LG", -split), ("RG", split), ("LT", -2 * split), ("RT", 2 * split),
                 ("LE", -3 * split), ("RE", 3 * split)]:
        pl_.append(O(k, "OL" if k[1] in "GT" else "TE", -0.7, w, ""))
    pl_ += [O("LW", "TE", -1.4, -3 * split - 1.3, ""), O("RW", "TE", -1.4, 3 * split + 1.3, ""),
            O("HOLD", "P", -8.0, 1.1, "Ho"), O("K", "K", -10.4, -2.1, "K")]
    return pl_


def block_unit():
    """Ten rushers (six on the left of the snapper, the legal maximum) and one player back for a fake."""
    left = [-0.75, -2.1, -3.5, -4.9, -6.5, -8.1]
    right = [0.75, 2.1, 3.5, 6.5]
    pl_ = [D(f"L{i}", "DL", 1.0, w) for i, w in enumerate(left)]
    pl_ += [D(f"R{i}", "DL", 1.0, w) for i, w in enumerate(right)]
    pl_ += [D("FAKE", "DB", 7.0, 2.0)]
    return pl_


def fg_actions(p, speed_edge=6.4):
    # protectors: step inside and hold the line (don't give ground)
    for k in ("LG", "RG", "LT", "RT", "LE", "RE"):
        w = p.players[k].w
        p.block(k, pts=[(-0.35, -0.3 * np.sign(w))])
    p.block("LW", pts=[(-0.5, -0.8)])
    p.block("RW", pts=[(-0.5, 0.8)])
    # interior rushers: driven into the line and stopped
    for k in ("L0", "L1", "L2", "L3", "R0", "R1", "R2"):
        w = p.players[k].w
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.1, -0.15 * np.sign(w))], speed=2.4)
    # edges: the inside edge on each side takes on the wing; the outermost man on the overload is free
    p.rush("L4", pts=[(-1.6, 0.5)], speed=2.6)
    p.rush("R3", pts=[(-1.6, -0.5)], speed=2.6)
    p.rush("L5", pts=[(-3.4, 1.4), (-6.3, 6.4)], speed=speed_edge, delay=0.05)
    return p


SPOT = (-8.0, 0.0)
fo = fg_actions(Play(fg_unit(), block_unit(), los=75, to_go=None))
fo.path("K", [(0.25, 0.3), (2.2, 1.25), (1.4, 0.75)], speed=2.6, delay=0.2)
fo.path("FAKE", [(-1.0, -0.6)], speed=1.5, delay=0.3)


def fg_ball(t):
    if t <= 0:
        return (0.0, 0.0)
    if t < 0.38:
        return lerp((0.0, 0.0), (-7.6, 0.6), t / 0.38)
    if t < 0.6:
        return lerp((-7.6, 0.6), SPOT, (t - 0.38) / 0.22)
    if t < 1.3:
        return SPOT
    return (SPOT[0] + 22.0 * (t - 1.3), 0.0)


fo_df = with_ball(fo, fg_ball, t_after=0.3)


def fo_notes(axes):
    strip_text(axes[1], fo, -5.0, 6.0, "snap\narrives", color=OC)
    strip_text(axes[2], fo, -5.0, 6.0, "ball down,\nkicker on 2nd step", color=OC)
    strip_text(axes[3], fo, -3.2, -9.4, "free edge:\nstill short", color=DC)
    strip_text(axes[3], fo, -4.6, 5.6, "kick away", color=OC)


show_strip(fo_df, times=[0.0, 0.4, 0.9, 1.3], annotate=fo_notes)
```

Why does a tenth of a second matter so much? Because the rushers are running a race against it. An
edge rusher who isn't blocked needs roughly a second and a half to cover the eight or nine yards to
the spot where he can get a hand on the ball. A 1.3-second operation beats him; a 1.5-second
operation, caused by a snap that arrives high or a holder who bobbles it, doesn't. That's why the
snapper, holder and kicker practice together every day, and why teams are reluctant to change any
one of them in midseason. When a team signs a new long snapper in November, watch its kicker's
numbers.

Two habits of the operation follow from that race. **Icing the kicker** is the defense's attempt to
break the rhythm: its coach calls a timeout a moment before the snap, so the kicker has to walk back
and wait. He can only do it once per kick, because the rules allow a team just one timeout in the
same dead-ball period, and a second one called to "freeze" the kicker is unsportsmanlike conduct, a
15-yard foul.[^ice] The whistle often comes too late to stop the play, and the kicker gets a free
practice swing. Going the other way, when the snap is bad or the holder fumbles it, there is no point
kicking a ball off the ground. The holder shouts a code word ("Fire!" in many systems), the ends and
wings release as receivers, and he scrambles to run or throw. It rarely works, but it beats a
certain block.

### Protection: a wall that must not bend

```{python}
#| label: fig-fg-protection
#| fig-cap: "Field-goal protection against a block unit that overloads the kicking team's left side (six on the line there, the most the rules allow on one side of the snapper). The seven blockers on the line stand almost shoulder to shoulder, step inside and hold their ground; the two wings, a yard behind and outside the ends, step out at 45 degrees to meet the first edge rusher. That leaves the outermost rusher on the overload free, but with the longest path. The shaded oval is the block point, a yard or two in front of the spot, where the rising ball is still low enough to reach. Rules also forbid a rusher from lining up over the snapper or running and leaping over the line."
fp_ = fg_actions(Play(fg_unit(), block_unit(), los=75, to_go=None))
fp_.highlight("L5", color=PURPLE)
fld = fp_.draw(window=(-12.5, 9.5), lateral=(-14.5, 14.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
ball_at(fld, fp_, *SPOT)
ball_arrow(fld, fp_, (0.0, 0.0), (-7.5, 0.55), lw=1.0)
bx, by = P_(fld, fp_, -6.2, 0.2)
fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((bx, by), 4.2, 2.0, fc=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.15, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=0.8,
                         ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=2))
say(fld, fp_, -5.7, 5.6, "block point", color=DC)
lead(fld, fp_, (-5.7, 4.0), (-6.1, 1.9))
say(fld, fp_, 3.0, 0.0, "blockers: step inside, don't give ground", color=OC)
say(fld, fp_, -3.6, 9.4, "wing: 45° step\nto the edge", color=OC)
say(fld, fp_, -6.8, -9.6, "free rusher:\nlongest path", color=DC)
say(fld, fp_, 5.4, -9.4, "overload: six on\none side (the limit)", color=DC)
say(fld, fp_, 8.4, 2.0, "one man back\nfor a fake", color=DC)
say(fld, fp_, -10.3, -5.4, "kicker (K)", color=OC)
say(fld, fp_, -9.4, 4.1, "holder (Ho)", color=OC)
plt.show()
```

Field-goal protection runs on a few blunt rules, and every one of them has a reason:

- **Tight splits.** The linemen stand almost foot to foot, much closer than on a normal play. There
  is no running lane to open, so there is no reason to leave gaps for rushers.
- **Step inside, protect inside.** Each blocker is responsible for the gap to his inside, toward the
  snapper. The kick goes straight up the middle, so a rusher in the middle has the shortest route to
  the ball's flight. Outside rushers have to travel farther and around bodies.
- **Don't give ground.** A blocker who gets pushed back a yard has moved the line of hands a yard
  closer to the rising ball. Interior rushers don't need to get *through*; they need to push the
  wall back far enough that a raised arm meets the ball. Big defensive linemen on block units try to
  do exactly that: collapse the middle and reach.
- **Wings take the edge.** The two wings set at an angle and meet the first rusher off each edge.
  Any extra rusher outside them is left free, because by the time he arrives the ball should be gone.
  That is the bet the 1.3-second operation is paying for.

The **block unit** on the other side has its own playbook: overload one side with as many rushers as
the rules allow, crash a big man into the snapper's gap, time the snap, and send the longest-armed
players at the block point. The rules put limits on it, mostly to protect players who can't defend
themselves. The snapper is the clearest case: his head is down between his legs at the snap, so the
rules treat him as a
[defenseless player](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd) until he has had a chance to protect
himself, and no defender within a yard of the line may line up over him.[^snapper] On field goals and
tries, no more than six defenders may be on the line on either side of the snapper, and nobody may
push a teammate into the formation.[^fgrules] Since 2017 a rusher may not take a running start and leap over the line to
block a kick, a play that had become popular and that blockers, rising from their stances, could flip
into a dangerous fall.[^leap] Blocks are rare anyway: `{python} S["fg_blk"]` of NFL field-goal
attempts from 2021 to 2025. When one happens, check the replay for three things: a low kick (the
kicker's fault), a blocker pushed back (the protection's fault), or a slow operation (the snap or
the hold).

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: the holder"}
Why not kick off a tee, as on kickoffs? The NFL's rules don't allow a tee on a field goal or
extra point,[^tee] so the ball has to be held, and the holder becomes a fourth specialist in the
operation: usually the punter, who has the best hands among the specialists, already catches long
snaps for a living, and practices with the kicker and snapper every day. The trade-off is one more pair of hands that can fail, and one more player who can run or
throw on a fake. Both matter later in this chapter.
:::

## The extra point, before and after 2015

You met the try after a touchdown in
[The Game in Fifteen Minutes](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd): kick
the [extra point](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd) for one point or run a
[two-point conversion](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd) from the 2 for
two. Mechanically, the extra point is just a short field goal: same snap, same hold, same
protection, same block units. What makes it worth a section is the experiment the league ran on it.

For decades the kick was snapped from the 2-yard line, a 20-yard kick. In 2014 kickers made
`{python} S["xp14"]` of them. A play that succeeds 99 times in 100 isn't really a play, and the
competition committee (the panel of team executives and coaches that proposes rule changes to the
owners) wanted the try to involve a decision. The league tested a longer kick in the
2014 preseason, and in May 2015 the owners voted 30–2 to snap the kick from the 15 (a 33-yard
kick), leave the two-point try at the 2, and let the defense score two points by returning a
blocked kick or a turnover on the try the length of the field.[^pat2015]

```{python}
#| label: tbl-try
#| tbl-cap: "The try before and after the 2015 change, regular seasons. The extra-point kick became a 33-yarder and stopped being automatic; two-point tries roughly doubled but remain a minority of tries. Every season to 2016 is shown, then every other season, plus 2025. Source: nflverse play-by-play (tries wiped out by penalties not counted)."
rows = []
for s in [2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024, 2025]:
    r = try_tab.loc[s]
    rows.append([s, f"{int(r.xp_att):,}", pct(r.xp_pct, 1), f"{int(r.tp_att)}", pct(r.tp_pct), pct(r.tp_share, 1)])
md_table(rows, ["Season", "Extra-point kicks", "Made", "Two-point tries", "Converted", "2-pt share"],
         [":---", "---:", "---:", "---:", "---:", "---:"])
```

The results, in three parts:[^patcalc]

1. **The kick got harder, but not hard.** Success dropped from `{python} S["xp14"]` in 2014 to
   `{python} S["xp15"]` in 2015, and has averaged `{python} S["xp_2125"]` from 2021 to 2025. A
   33-yard kick is still easy for an NFL kicker; the misses come from wind, cold, bad snaps and blocks
   (`{python} S["xpblk_1014"]` blocked extra points a season in 2010–2014, `{python} S["xpblk_1525"]` a
   season since). The snap and the hold are the same distance from the line as before, so why more
   blocks? There is no clean answer. Since 2015 a blocked kick can be returned for two points, so
   block units have a reason to rush every try as if it mattered, and the yearly counts are small and
   jumpy (anywhere from `{python} S["xpblk_lo"]` to `{python} S["xpblk_hi"]` a season since 2015).
2. **The two options became nearly equal.** Since 2015 two-point tries have succeeded
   `{python} S["tp_pct_1525"]` of the time, worth about `{python} S["tp_val"]` points per try, against
   about `{python} S["xp_val"]` for the kick. When two options are worth the same on average, the
   choice turns on the *score* and on how good your offense is from the 2, and that is a real
   decision.
3. **Two-point tries roughly doubled.** From about `{python} S["tp_1014"]` a season in 2010–2014
   (`{python} S["tp14"]` in 2014) to `{python} S["tp15"]` in 2015 and about `{python} S["tp_2125"]` a
   season in 2021–2025. The most aggressive team since 2015 is `{python} S["tp_top"]`. Still, it's
   only about one try in ten: most coaches, offered two choices with the same average, take the
   safer, more predictable one, except when the scoreboard says otherwise. (Single seasons bounce
   around: the two-point rate was `{python} S["tp23"]` in 2023 and `{python} S["tp24"]` in 2024, but
   with only about `{python} S["tp_2125"]` tries a year, a season's rate is uncertain by roughly
   ±`{python} S["tp_moe"]` points, so swings like that are mostly noise.)

When does the scoreboard say otherwise? Count the margin *after* the touchdown's six points. If you
now trail by 2, a two-pointer ties the game and a kick doesn't. If you now trail by 5, a two-pointer
makes it a 3-point game, so a field goal can tie. The best-known modern call comes when you trail by
14 late and score: you now trail by 8, and analytics favor going for two *right away*. Make it (about
half the time) and the next touchdown plus a kick wins the game in regulation. Miss it and you need a
two-pointer after the next touchdown just to tie, but you know that while there is still time to plan
for it. Over the two tries, going for two first gives roughly a coin-flip chance of winning without
overtime; kicking twice almost guarantees overtime. The full table, the "two-point chart," and that
arithmetic live in
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd),
and the plays teams run from the 2 are in
[Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd).

## The punt: field position for sale

A [punt](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) gives the ball to the
other team on purpose, as far down the field as possible.
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)
explained the trade: you were probably going to lose the ball on fourth down anyway, so you
sell possession for roughly 40 yards of
[field position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd). Now we look at
how the sale is made, because a punt is a three-part play: **protect** the punter for two seconds,
**kick** the ball where the coverage can reach it, and **cover** 40-plus yards of field before the
returner can do anything with it. Every punt formation is a different answer to one tension:
players who stay home to block can't run downfield to cover.

### The punt operation

The punter stands about 14 to 15 yards behind the line. The long snapper's target is about
**0.7 seconds** to the punter's hands; the punter takes a step or two and kicks, and the whole thing,
snap to kick, is aimed at about **2.0 seconds**. A good NFL punt then hangs in the air about 4.5 to
5 seconds.[^puntops] Those three numbers explain almost everything about punt formations. The
blockers need to hold up rushers for about two seconds, and the coverage has about four and a half
seconds after the kick to get 40 yards downfield.

**Hang time** (how long the ball is in the air) matters as much as distance. A 50-yard punt that
hangs 3.8 seconds gives a returner a head start on the coverage; a 44-yarder that hangs 5 seconds
lands with gunners standing next to him. The greatest punter in the sport's history, Ray Guy of the
Oakland Raiders (1973–86), was famous for exactly this: kicks so high that broadcasters timed them,
and that made him the first pure punter elected to the Hall of Fame.[^guy]

### Formations: tight, spread, and what "shield" means

```{python}
#| label: fig-punt-formations
#| fig-cap: "The two NFL punt formations at the same scale. Left, a tight punt, now a backed-up or emergency look: everybody in close like a field-goal unit, with two wings and a personal protector (PP) in front of the punter (P). It is the safest protection and the slowest coverage. Right, the NFL's base spread punt: the gunners (G) split wide on the line, five interior linemen, two wings a yard behind the line just outside the tackles, and the personal protector about six yards deep. The wings and the PP (dotted triangle) are the shield, the last wall between a rusher and the punter."
def tight_punt():
    pl_ = [O("LS", "C", -0.7, 0.0, "LS")]
    for k, w in [("LG", -1.4), ("RG", 1.4), ("LT", -2.8), ("RT", 2.8), ("LE", -4.2), ("RE", 4.2)]:
        pl_.append(O(k, "OL", -0.7, w, ""))
    pl_ += [O("LW", "TE", -1.5, -5.5, ""), O("RW", "TE", -1.5, 5.5, ""),
            O("PP", "FB", -6.0, 0.9, "PP"), O("P", "P", -14.5, 0.0, "P")]
    return pl_


def spread_punt(gw=19.5):
    """The NFL's base punt: gunners on the ends of the line, five interior linemen, two wings a yard
    behind the line outside the tackles, the personal protector about six yards deep."""
    pl_ = [O("LS", "C", -0.7, 0.0, "LS")]
    for k, w in [("LG", -1.7), ("RG", 1.7), ("LT", -3.4), ("RT", 3.4)]:
        pl_.append(O(k, "OL", -0.7, w, ""))
    pl_ += [O("LW", "TE", -1.6, -4.7, ""), O("RW", "TE", -1.6, 4.7, ""),
            O("PP", "FB", -6.2, 1.0, "PP"), O("P", "P", -14.5, 0.0, "P"),
            O("GL", "WR", -0.7, -gw, "G"), O("GR", "WR", -0.7, gw, "G")]
    return pl_


fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [20, 46]})
t1 = Play(tight_punt(), [], los=30, to_go=None)
f1 = t1.draw(ax=a1, window=(-17.0, 2.5), lateral=(-10.0, 10.0), title=False)
no_numbers(f1)
t2 = Play(spread_punt(), [], los=30, to_go=None)
f2 = t2.draw(ax=a2, window=(-17.0, 2.5), lateral=(-23.0, 23.0), title=False)
no_numbers(f2)
a1.set_title("Tight punt (backed up)", fontsize=9, loc="left")
a2.set_title("Spread punt (the NFL base)", fontsize=9, loc="left")
# the shield: a dotted triangle joining the two wings and the personal protector
tri = [P_(f2, t2, -1.6, -4.7), P_(f2, t2, -1.6, 4.7), P_(f2, t2, -6.2, 1.0), P_(f2, t2, -1.6, -4.7)]
a2.plot([q[0] for q in tri], [q[1] for q in tri], color=OC, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (1.5, 1.5)), zorder=2.5)
say(f2, t2, -3.4, -19.5, "gunner", color=OC, fs=6)
say(f2, t2, -3.4, 19.5, "gunner", color=OC, fs=6)
say(f2, t2, -6.4, 6.9, "personal protector", color=OC, fs=6)
say(f2, t2, -14.5, 4.6, "punter", color=OC, fs=6)
say(f2, t2, -4.4, -9.4, "wing", color=OC, fs=6)
lead(f2, t2, (-3.8, -8.3), (-2.0, -5.3))
say(f2, t2, -4.4, 11.2, "wing", color=OC, fs=6)
lead(f2, t2, (-3.8, 10.1), (-2.0, 5.3))
say(f2, t2, -7.4, -6.4, "the shield:\nwings + PP", color=OC, fs=6)
lead(f2, t2, (-6.3, -4.6), (-4.3, -2.5))
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The oldest answer is the **tight punt**: everyone packed in close to block, like a field-goal unit,
then everyone runs. It is nearly unblockable and covers slowly, so today you see it mainly when a
team is backed up inside its own 10, where a blocked punt is likely a touchdown or a
[safety](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd) for the other team. Backed up,
the end line squeezes the punter too. With the ball at the 2, the back of the end zone is only 12
yards behind the line, so he can't stand his usual 14 or 15 yards deep; he sets up a step in front
of the end line, the snap arrives sooner, and the rushers have less ground to cover. If a snap sails
over his head there, his first job is to fall on the ball: a punter tackled in his own end zone, or a
ball that skids out of the back of it, is a safety. Late in a game a team sometimes concedes an
[intentional safety](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd) on purpose: two
points for the opponent, in exchange for kicking the ball away from safer ground instead of punting
from under its own goal posts.

Everywhere else, the NFL lines up in the **spread punt** (the right of the figure). The two outside
men on the line, the gunners, split wide near the sidelines. Five interior linemen (the snapper, two
guards and two tackles) stand on the line with a little more space between them than on a field
goal. Two wings line up a yard behind the line, just outside the tackles, and one more man, the
[**personal protector**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-personal-protector), stands five to seven
yards deep. He is the punt team's quarterback: he checks the return team's alignment, calls the
protection ("watch the overload left!"), blocks whoever comes free, and he is the most common ball
carrier on a fake punt. Most units block with a zone or "slide" scheme: each lineman takes a gap,
and the personal protector picks out the most dangerous rusher and slides the protection toward
him, so that the man left unblocked is the one with the longest path to the ball.

Where does "shield" come in? The [**shield punt**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shield-punt)
(also called the [**spread punt**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spread-punt); the two names are
used loosely and overlap) is named for its last line of protection: blockers standing a few yards in
front of the punter who wall off any rusher well before the spot where the ball leaves his foot. In
the NFL that shield is the two wings and the personal protector, the dotted triangle in the figure.
The version with three blockers standing side by side a few yards behind the line, which you'll see
on college Saturdays, grew up in college football, and some NFL teams borrow it. The two levels
differ because of one rule.

Under the NFL's rules, only the two end men on the line (the gunners, as long as they are the widest
players on each side) may run downfield before the ball is kicked; everyone else may not go more
than a yard past the line until the kick.[^release] The rule dates from 1974, when the league, trying
to revive punt returns, first barred *every* punt-team player from releasing early and then, after
coaches complained, carved out the two men on the ends.[^punt74] College has no such restriction, so
a college punt team can release its whole line at the snap and trust the shield to stop anyone who
gets through. So what does the shield buy an NFL team, whose linemen must wait anyway? Protection
with fewer bodies and shorter blocks. With the wings and the personal protector behind them, the
linemen don't have to win their blocks; they only have to slow a rusher for two seconds, then turn
and run the instant they hear the foot hit the ball. NFL punt coverage is therefore built around the
gunners.

### Gunners and vices

The [gunner](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) is the punt team's missile, and the
return team's answer is the [**vice**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-vice) (also called a
[**jammer**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jammer)): a blocker, usually a cornerback, who
lines up across from a gunner and tries to keep him from getting downfield, by jamming him at the
line and then running with him and shoving him toward the sideline. Most return teams put two vices
on each gunner, one on either side of him, so the gunner can't simply run around one. That costs
the return team four players, which is why the gunner is worth so much: one great gunner ties up
two opponents on every punt. (Coaches usually spell it "vise," like the tool, and strictly they use
the word for the two-man bracket; a lone blocker on a gunner is a "jammer" or a "single jam." The
Big Data Bowl files spell it "vises.")

Watch a gunner on the replay and you'll see a little wrestling match on the sideline: the gunner
trying to swim past one vice (a quick arm-over move) or "stack" him (get even with him and step
directly in front of his path, so the vice is stuck behind), the vices trying to run him out of
bounds. The vices can be this rough because the usual pass-defense limits are relaxed here: against
a punt formation, contact on the end men that would normally be illegal contact or pass interference
is allowed before the kick, as long as it isn't holding.[^vicecontact] A gunner who voluntarily runs
out of bounds to avoid a block commits a foul, and one who has been out of bounds, even if he was
pushed, may not be the first player to touch the punt when he comes back in.[^oob]

```{python}
#| label: fig-shield-punt
#| fig-cap: "A spread punt from the kicking team's own 30 under NFL release rules, simulated tracking in Big Data Bowl format (an illustrative play, not a real one). Snap: the gunners (G) wide, each with two vices (V); five linemen; the wings and personal protector (PP) form the shield; the punter (P) about 14 yards deep; the returner (PR) about 45 yards past the line, some 60 yards from the punter. 2.0 s: the kick. The gunners, the only players allowed to leave early, are already 10 to 12 yards downfield with their vices riding them; the linemen and wings release now. 4.2 s: the ball is in the air, and the coverage spreads into lanes about five yards apart so the returner has no seam. 6.4 s: the ball arrives with a gunner on each side of the returner and the lanes closing; the punter and PP trail as the last safeties. The return team is shown in its simplest plan, a token rush and then a retreat for a fair catch, so it sets no blocks."
def return_team(ret_d=45.0, gw=20.0):
    """A return team: six men on the line, two vices on each gunner, one returner deep."""
    pl_ = [D(f"F{i}", "DL", 1.0, w) for i, w in enumerate([-5.5, -3.0, -1.0, 1.0, 3.0, 5.5])]
    pl_ += [D("VL1", "CB", 1.0, -gw + 1.8, "V"), D("VL2", "CB", 1.0, -gw - 1.8, "V"),
            D("VR1", "CB", 1.0, gw - 1.8, "V"), D("VR2", "CB", 1.0, gw + 1.8, "V"),
            D("PR", "DB", ret_d, 0.0, "PR")]
    return pl_


sp = Play(spread_punt(gw=20.0), return_team(ret_d=45.0, gw=20.0), los=40, to_go=None)
KICK_T, CATCH_T = 2.0, 6.4
RET = (45.0, 1.5)
KICK_SPOT = (-12.9, 0.0)
# gunners: fight through the vices at the line, then bend in toward the returner
sp.route("GL", [(4.0, -19.4), (20.0, -15.5), (42.5, -2.0)], absolute=True, speed=7.3)
sp.route("GR", [(4.0, 19.4), (20.0, 15.5), (42.5, 5.0)], absolute=True, speed=7.3)
# vices ride their gunner: the outside vice on his outside hip, the inside vice on his inside hip
for k, side, out in (("VL1", -1, False), ("VL2", -1, True), ("VR1", 1, False), ("VR2", 1, True)):
    dw = 1.5 if out else -1.5
    sp.path(k, [(3.5, side * (19.4 + dw)), (19.0, side * (15.5 + dw)), (40.0, side * (4.5 + dw) + 1.5)],
            absolute=True, speed=6.6)
# linemen and wings: hold up the rush until the kick, then release into lanes about five yards apart
LANES = {"LW": -14.0, "LT": -9.0, "LG": -4.5, "LS": 0.0, "RG": 4.5, "RT": 9.0, "RW": 14.0}
for k, lane in LANES.items():
    sp.block(k, pts=[(-0.4, 0.0)], speed=1.0)                      # 0.4 s set, then hold
    sp.path(k, [(6.0, lane * 0.9), (33.0, lane * 0.75 + 0.4)], absolute=True, speed=7.0,
            delay=KICK_T - 0.4 - 0.1)
sp.block("PP", pts=[(0.0, -0.3)], speed=1.0)
sp.path("PP", [(3.0, 1.0), (17.0, 3.5)], absolute=True, speed=5.5, delay=KICK_T - 0.3 + 0.2)
# punter: catches the snap, takes his steps to the spot of the kick, then trails the coverage
sp.path("P", [KICK_SPOT], absolute=True, speed=1.2, delay=0.75)    # arrives about 2.1 s
sp.path("P", [(4.0, -3.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.0, delay=0.4)
# front six: a token rush, then turn and retreat toward the returner
for i, k in enumerate(["F0", "F1", "F2", "F3", "F4", "F5"]):
    q = sp.players[k]
    sp.rush(k, pts=[(-0.9, 0.0)], speed=1.2)
    sp.path(k, [(18.0 + 1.5 * (i % 2), q.w * 1.6), (26.0 + 1.5 * (i % 2), q.w * 1.3)], absolute=True,
            speed=5.8, delay=0.1)
sp.path("PR", [RET], absolute=True, speed=1.5, delay=4.6)


def punt_ball(t):
    if t <= 0:
        return (0.0, 0.0)
    if t < 0.75:
        return lerp((0.0, 0.0), (-14.2, 0.0), t / 0.75)
    if t < KICK_T:
        return lerp((-14.2, 0.0), KICK_SPOT, (t - 0.75) / (KICK_T - 0.75))
    if t < CATCH_T:
        return lerp(KICK_SPOT, RET, (t - KICK_T) / (CATCH_T - KICK_T))
    return RET


sp_df = with_ball(sp, punt_ball, t_after=0.4)


def sp_notes(axes):
    strip_text(axes[0], sp, 20.0, 0.0, "returner 45 yds\npast the line,\n~60 from punter", color=DC, fs=6.4)
    strip_text(axes[0], sp, -3.6, -18.0, "G + 2 V", color=OC, fs=6.4)
    strip_text(axes[0], sp, -3.6, 18.0, "G + 2 V", color=OC, fs=6.4)
    strip_text(axes[0], sp, -9.5, -7.5, "shield:\nwings + PP", color=OC, fs=6.4)
    strip_text(axes[0], sp, -14.5, 7.0, "punter", color=OC, fs=6.4)
    strip_text(axes[1], sp, 18.0, 0.0, "kick: linemen\nrelease now", color=OC, fs=6.4)
    ax = axes[2]
    for lane in LANES.values():
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = sxy(sp, 12.0, lane * 0.87), sxy(sp, 30.0, lane * 0.77)
        ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=OC, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (1, 2)), alpha=0.8, zorder=2)
    strip_text(ax, sp, 36.0, -14.0, "coverage\nlanes", color=OC, fs=6.4)
    strip_text(axes[3], sp, 20.0, 12.5, "ball arrives:\na gunner on\neach side of PR", color=OC, fs=6.4)


show_strip(sp_df, times=[0.0, KICK_T, 4.2, CATCH_T], annotate=sp_notes)
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the same picture from real tracking: 2022 Big Data Bowl punts)"
#| eval: false
# Not run when the book builds: the data isn't bundled. The 2022 Big Data Bowl was about special teams:
# every punt, kickoff and field goal of 2018-2020 with tracking, plus PFF scouting data that times the
# operation (snapTime, operationTime, hangTime) and names the gunners, vises and punt rushers by jersey.
# Download: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2022/data  ->  data/bdb2022/
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb2022/tracking2020.csv")
games = pd.read_csv("data/bdb2022/games.csv")
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb2022/plays.csv")
pff = pd.read_csv("data/bdb2022/PFFScoutingData.csv")

# 2022 tracking marks the teams "home"/"away"; give prepare() the club codes it compares to possessionTeam
trk = trk.merge(games[["gameId", "homeTeamAbbr", "visitorTeamAbbr"]], on="gameId")
trk["club"] = np.select([trk.club.eq("home"), trk.club.eq("away")],
                        [trk.homeTeamAbbr, trk.visitorTeamAbbr], default="football")

punts = plays[plays.specialTeamsPlayType.eq("Punt")].merge(pff, on=["gameId", "playId"])
print(punts[["operationTime", "hangTime"]].describe())   # check this chapter's ~2.0 s and ~4.5 s
one = punts[punts.specialTeamsResult.eq("Return") & punts.vises.str.count(";").ge(3)].iloc[0]
print(one.playDescription, "| gunners:", one.gunners, "| vises:", one.vises)
show_animation(bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=one.gameId, play_id=one.playId), times=[0, 2.0, 4.2, 6.0])
```

The coverage is a zone defense run backward. The players fan out into **lanes**, each about five
yards wide, so that wherever the returner goes there is someone in front of him; the gunners
attack from the outside and force him back toward the middle; the punter and the personal protector
hang back as the last line, like safeties. A coverage player who runs straight at the ball and
leaves his lane opens a seam, and a seam is how a punt becomes a touchdown.

### Where to aim: directional, coffin-corner and pooch punts

A punter isn't only trying to kick it far. From deep in his own territory he wants distance and
hang time. From midfield the problem flips: there is too *little* field, and a ball that bounces
into the end zone is a [**touchback**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-touchback), with the
receiving team starting at its own 20 (a punt touchback is still the 20, unlike the kickoff's 35).
A touchback from the opponent's 40 has bought only 20 yards of field position. Three kinds of punts
answer different versions of that problem.

```{python}
#| label: fig-directional
#| fig-cap: "Where punters aim. Left, from the opponent's 42: a coffin-corner punt (1) angles out of bounds near the 6, giving the returner nothing; a high pooch punt (2) lands around the 9 with gunners arriving to down it; a ball kicked too far (3) bounces into the end zone for a touchback at the 20. Right, from the kicking team's own 25: a directional punt of 45-plus yards toward the numbers puts the returner near the sideline, so the coverage only has to squeeze him from one side; the sideline acts as an extra tackler."
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.6))
L = 68.0            # line of scrimmage at the opponent's 42 (BDB x)
fA = Field(ax=a1, orient="vertical", los=L, window=(-30.0, 52.0), to_go=None)
PX, PY = L - 14.0, MIDDLE


def arc(fld, x0, y0, x1, y1, rad, col=style.BALL, lw=1.3):
    (ax0, ay0), (ax1, ay1) = fld.xy(x0, y0), fld.xy(x1, y1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(ax0), float(ay0)), (float(ax1), float(ay1)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                     mutation_scale=9, color=col, lw=lw, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=6,
                                     connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}"))


def mark(fld, x, y, side, label):
    px, py = fld.xy(x, y)
    draw_marker(fld.ax, float(px), float(py), side, label, fld.pts_per_yard())


def txt(fld, x, y, s, color=style.INK_2, fs=6.4, ha="center"):
    px, py = fld.xy(x, y)
    fld.ax.text(float(px), float(py), s, fontsize=fs, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9, linespacing=1.1,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


mark(fA, PX, PY, "off", "P")
arc(fA, PX, PY, 104.0, 0.4, -0.10)                 # (1) coffin corner, out near the 6
arc(fA, PX, PY, 101.0, MIDDLE - 1.0, -0.03)        # (2) pooch to the 9
arc(fA, PX, PY, 115.0, 37.0, 0.12)                 # (3) too long: into the end zone
mark(fA, 100.0, MIDDLE - 4.5, "off", "G")
mark(fA, 99.5, MIDDLE + 2.5, "off", "G")
mark(fA, 105.0, MIDDLE + 3.5, "def", "PR")
txt(fA, 106.5, 8.5, "1 coffin\ncorner")
txt(fA, 94.0, MIDDLE - 9.5, "2 pooch:\ndowned at 9")
txt(fA, 115.5, 21.0, "3 touchback (to the 20)")
txt(fA, PX + 2.0, PY + 7.5, "punt from\nopp. 42", color=OC)
a1.set_title("Pin them deep", fontsize=9, loc="left")

L2 = 35.0           # own 25
fB = Field(ax=a2, orient="vertical", los=L2, window=(-16.0, 66.0), to_go=None)
PX2 = L2 - 14.0
mark(fB, PX2, MIDDLE, "off", "P")
arc(fB, PX2, MIDDLE, 83.0, 9.5, 0.12)
mark(fB, 83.0, 9.5, "def", "PR")
for (x, y) in [(77.0, 3.5), (76.5, 16.5), (72.0, 22.0), (70.0, 28.0), (68.0, 34.5)]:
    mark(fB, x, y, "off", "")
```
