```{python}
for x, y, dx, dy in [(77.0, 3.5, 4.0, 3.0), (76.5, 16.5, 4.0, -3.0), (72.0, 22.0, 6.0, -6.0),
                     (70.0, 28.0, 6.0, -9.0), (68.0, 34.5, 7.0, -12.0)]:
    (sx, sy), (ex, ey) = fB.xy(x, y), fB.xy(x + dx, y + dy)
    a2.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(sx), float(sy)), (float(ex), float(ey)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                 mutation_scale=7, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=5))
(rx0, ry0), (rx1, ry1) = fB.xy(79.0, 0.0), fB.xy(91.0, 9.5)
a2.add_patch(Rectangle((min(rx0, rx1), min(ry0, ry1)), abs(rx1 - rx0), abs(ry1 - ry0), fc=style.DEFENSE,
                       alpha=0.10, ec="none", zorder=1))
txt(fB, 95.3, 7.0, "little room\nto this side", color=DC)
txt(fB, 88.0, 31.0, "coverage squeezes\nfrom one side", color=OC)
txt(fB, PX2 + 2.0, MIDDLE + 7.5, "punt from\nown 25", color=OC)
a2.set_title("Directional: use the sideline", fontsize=9, loc="left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- A **directional punt** is aimed toward one sideline instead of the middle of the field. It gives up
  a few yards of distance to put the returner where he has room on only one side, so the coverage
  can squeeze him with the sideline acting as an extra tackler. Most NFL punts from a team's own
  territory are directional in this sense; punters practice hitting the numbers on either side.
- A [**coffin-corner punt**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-coffin-corner-punt) is the old art of
  kicking the ball out of bounds just short of the goal line, near the corner. A ball kicked out of
  bounds is dead where it crosses the sideline, with no return and no touchback.[^oobpunt] The catch
  is precision: miss by a few yards one way and the ball goes into the end zone; miss the other way
  and it stays in bounds for the returner.
- A [**pooch punt**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pooch-punt) is the modern answer from near
  midfield: a deliberately short, very high kick, often struck so the ball turns end over end and
  "checks up" (bounces backward or dies) instead of rolling forward. It lands around the 10, the
  returner usually lets it go or fair-catches it, and the gunners down it before it reaches the end
  zone. From the opponent's 40–50 in 2021–2025, `{python} S["mid_in10"]` of NFL punts finished inside
  the 10 and `{python} S["mid_tb"]` went for touchbacks (`{python} S["mid_n"]` punts).

The pooch has largely replaced the coffin corner. In 2021–2025 only `{python} S["oob10"]` of all
punts went out of bounds inside the 10, against `{python} S["down10"]` that were downed there. A big
reason is the Australian invasion: since Darren Bennett, an Australian rules football player, began
punting for the San Diego Chargers in 1995, a steady stream of Australians (many trained by the
ProKick Australia program) has brought end-over-end and spinning kicks that make the ball stop
where they want it.[^aussie] The same tradition gave the NFL the
[**rugby punt**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rugby-punt): the punter takes the snap, rolls out
toward one side like a quarterback, and kicks on the run, usually a low, end-over-end ball that
bounces and rolls. It buys time against the rush (the rushers aimed at the spot where a normal punt
is kicked), it makes the ball miserable to field, and it carries a threat: if the edge is open, the
punter can tuck it and run.

### Measuring a punt: gross, net and where it lands

A punter's *gross* average is how far his kicks travel from the line of scrimmage. The number that
matters for field position is the
[**net punting average**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-net-punting-average): gross distance minus
return yards, minus 20 yards for every touchback (because the ball comes back out to the 20),
divided by the number of punts. One bookkeeping convention matters: a punt that goes into the end
zone is credited with its distance *to the goal line*, not to wherever it landed. Net is what the punt team, kicker and coverage together, actually
bought.

```{python}
#| label: fig-net-trend
#| fig-cap: "NFL punting, 1999–2025 regular seasons: gross average (how far punts travel) and net average (after returns and touchbacks). Both rose about six yards. The gap between them, mostly return yards, has narrowed slightly, because returners fair-catch more and coverage units have improved. Source: nflverse play-by-play (blocked punts count as zero yards in the net)."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
ax.plot(trend.index, trend.gross, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, marker="o", ms=3, label="Gross average")
ax.plot(trend.index, trend.net, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2, marker="o", ms=3, label="Net average")
ax.fill_between(trend.index, trend.net, trend.gross, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.5, lw=0)
ax.text(2011.5, (trend.gross[2011] + trend.net[2011]) / 2, "returns and\ntouchbacks", fontsize=7.5,
        color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center")
for s in (1999, 2025):
    ax.text(s + (0.4 if s == 2025 else -0.4), trend.gross[s] + 0.9, f"{trend.gross[s]:.1f}", fontsize=7.5,
            color=style.SERIES[0], ha="left" if s == 2025 else "right")
    ax.text(s + (0.4 if s == 2025 else -0.4), trend.net[s] - 1.2, f"{trend.net[s]:.1f}", fontsize=7.5,
            color=style.SERIES[1], ha="left" if s == 2025 else "right")
ax.set_xlim(1996.5, 2027.5)
ax.set_ylim(31, 50)
ax.set_ylabel("yards per punt")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

In 1999 the average NFL punt traveled `{python} S["gross99"]` yards and netted `{python} S["net99"]`;
in 2025 it traveled `{python} S["gross25"]` and netted `{python} S["net25"]`.[^puntcalc] The gap between
gross and net, mostly return yards, shrank from about `{python} S["ret_9903"]` yards a punt in
1999–2003 to `{python} S["ret_2125"]` in 2021–2025, as fair catches rose from `{python} S["fc99"]` of
punts to `{python} S["fc25"]`. Teams also punt less: `{python} S["punts99"]` punts in 1999,
`{python} S["punts25"]` in 2025, as offenses improved and coaches went for it more on fourth down.

```{python}
#| label: fig-punt-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Where punts end, by where they are kicked from (2021–2025 regular seasons, blocked punts excluded). Each column is one band of line of scrimmage and sums to 100%; each cell is the share of those punts whose kick ended in that band of the receiving team's field (caught, downed, out of bounds or rolling dead, before any return). From deep in their own territory punters drive it 45-plus yards; once past midfield the ball piles up between the receiving team's 5 and 15, and the touchback row darkens. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
hm = recent.copy()
X_EDGES = [100, 90, 80, 70, 60, 50, 40, 30]
X_LABS = ["own\n1–10", "own\n11–20", "own\n21–30", "own\n31–40", "own\n41–50", "opp.\n49–40", "opp.\n39–30"]
hm["xb"] = pd.cut(hm.yardline_100, X_EDGES[::-1], labels=X_LABS[::-1], right=False)
Y_EDGES = [0.5, 5.5, 10.5, 15.5, 20.5, 25.5, 30.5, 35.5, 40.5, 50.5, 101]
Y_LABS = ["1–5", "6–10", "11–15", "16–20", "21–25", "26–30", "31–35", "36–40", "41–50", "51+"]
hm["yb"] = pd.cut(hm.fin, Y_EDGES, labels=Y_LABS)
hm["yb"] = hm.yb.cat.add_categories(["touchback"])
hm.loc[hm.touchback == 1, "yb"] = "touchback"
grid = pd.crosstab(hm.yb, hm.xb, normalize="columns").reindex(index=["touchback"] + Y_LABS, columns=X_LABS)
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("rtg_blue", [style.SURFACE] + style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.2))
ax.imshow(grid.values * 100, cmap=cmap, aspect="auto", vmin=0, vmax=45)
for i in range(grid.shape[0]):
    for j in range(grid.shape[1]):
        v = grid.values[i, j]
        if v >= 0.02:
            ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.0%}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7,
                    color="white" if v > 0.24 else style.INK)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(X_LABS)), X_LABS, fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(grid.index)), ["end zone\n(touchback)"] + [f"their {s}" for s in Y_LABS[:-1]] + ["kicking team's\nside of 50"], fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("punted from (line of scrimmage)")
ax.set_ylabel("kick ended at")

    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)

```

Read the heatmap column by column and you can see the punter's job change. From his own 11–20 the
kicks end anywhere from the opponent's 21 to past midfield; distance is everything. By the
opponent's 49–40 the kicks bunch up inside the receiving team's 15, with a real share in the end zone
for touchbacks. That's the pooch at work, and the touchback row is the cost of missing it. A punt
from deep in your own end, on average, ends near the receiving team's
`{python} S["deep_fin"]`; the return, if any, comes on top.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"A longer punt is a better punt." Not past midfield, and not even always from deep. A 60-yard line
drive that gets returned 20 yards nets 40; a 45-yarder with 5 seconds of hang time that is
fair-caught nets 45. A punt from the opponent's 45 that rolls into the end zone goes in the books as 45 yards (to the
goal line) and nets only 25, because the ball comes out to the 20.
Judge a punt by where the receiving team *starts*, not by the number on the graphic.
:::

## The return team: return, block, or play it safe

Now flip to the other side. On every punt the receiving team makes a choice before the snap, and
the alignment usually gives it away.

### The return

Most of the time the return team wants a return, or at least a clean fair catch. Its two biggest
jobs are to slow the gunners (the vices) and to hold up the interior coverage long enough to give the
returner room. The most recognizable design is the
[**return wall**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-return-wall) (or
[**wall return**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wall-return)): after a token rush to keep the
punt team honest, most of the return team peels back toward one sideline and forms a line of blockers
running parallel to it, about five yards apart. The returner catches the ball, heads for the wall,
and runs up the field behind it while the blockers turn and seal the coverage players inside. A
**middle return** does the opposite: blockers take on the coverage man in their lane and try to
open a seam straight up the field.

```{python}
#| label: fig-return-vs-safe
#| fig-cap: "Two return-team plans against the same spread punt. Left, a return wall: after a brief rush, five of the front six peel back to the punt team's left (the returner's right) and set a wall parallel to the sideline. On that side the two vices drive their gunner toward the sideline, out of the returner's lane; on the far side the vices ride the other gunner, one on each hip. The returner (PR) catches the ball and runs up the sideline behind the wall. Right, punt safe on fourth-and-short near midfield: the defense keeps its regular defenders on, covers every eligible punt-team player man to man (dotted lines: cornerbacks, CB, on the gunners; safeties, S, on the wings; a linebacker, LB, on the personal protector; the other linebacker spying the punter), holds its four-man front at the line against a direct snap, and gives up the return to make sure the punt team doesn't keep the ball."
def safe_team(gw=19.5):
    pl_ = [D(f"F{i}", "DL", 1.0, w) for i, w in enumerate([-4.6, -1.0, 1.0, 4.6])]
    pl_ += [D("LB1", "LB", 4.0, -3.5, "LB"), D("LB2", "LB", 4.0, 3.5, "LB"),
            D("C1", "CB", 1.0, -gw + 0.8, "CB"), D("C2", "CB", 1.0, gw - 0.8, "CB"),
            D("S1", "S", 6.5, -6.0, "S"), D("S2", "S", 6.5, 6.0, "S"), D("PR", "DB", 40.0, 0.0, "PR")]
    return pl_


fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.3))
rw = Play(spread_punt(), return_team(ret_d=40.0, gw=19.5), los=30, to_go=None)
# five of the front six peel back to the punt team's left and set the wall; one rushes
for k, (d, w) in {"F1": (10.0, -16.5), "F2": (16.0, -17.0), "F3": (22.0, -17.5), "F4": (28.0, -18.0),
                  "F5": (34.0, -18.5)}.items():
    rw.path(k, [(0.2, rw.players[k].w), (d, w)], absolute=True)
rw.path("F0", [(-1.5, -3.2)], absolute=True)
# wall side: the two vices drive their gunner toward the sideline, out of the returner's lane
rw.route("GL", [(4.0, -21.5), (8.0, -24.6)], absolute=True)
rw.path("VL1", [(4.5, -20.0), (8.6, -23.1)], absolute=True)
rw.path("VL2", [(5.0, -23.0), (9.6, -25.6)], absolute=True)
# far side: the vices ride the gunner, one on each hip, as he heads for the returner
rw.route("GR", [(8.0, 19.0), (28.0, 9.0)], absolute=True)
rw.path("VR2", [(8.0, 20.6), (27.0, 10.6)], absolute=True)
rw.path("VR1", [(7.0, 17.4), (25.0, 7.6)], absolute=True)
rw.run("PR", [(38.0, -10.0), (34.5, -22.0), (14.0, -22.5)], absolute=True)
fr = rw.draw(ax=a1, window=(-16.0, 45.0), lateral="full", title=False)
no_numbers(fr)
say(fr, rw, 20.0, -13.2, "wall", color=DC, fs=6.4, weight="bold")
say(fr, rw, 42.6, 0.0, "PR catches", color=DC, fs=6.0)
say(fr, rw, 40.5, -19.0, "PR runs\nbehind it", color=DC, fs=6.0)
say(fr, rw, -5.0, -20.5, "vices drive G\nto the sideline", color=DC, fs=6.0)
say(fr, rw, 13.0, 22.0, "vices\nride G", color=DC, fs=6.0)
a1.set_title("Return wall", fontsize=9, loc="left")

ps = Play(spread_punt(), safe_team(), los=30, to_go=None)
for d_, o_ in [("C1", "GL"), ("C2", "GR"), ("S1", "LW"), ("S2", "RW"), ("LB1", "PP"), ("LB2", "P")]:
    ps.man(d_, o_)
fs_ = ps.draw(ax=a2, window=(-16.0, 45.0), lateral="full", title=False)
no_numbers(fs_)
say(fs_, ps, 14.0, 0.0, "every eligible player\ncovered; front\nholds the line", color=DC, fs=6.2)
say(fs_, ps, 34.5, 0.0, "returner still\nback, but no wall", color=DC, fs=6.2)
say(fs_, ps, -10.0, 8.2, "LB spies\nthe punter", color=DC, fs=6.0)
a2.set_title("Punt safe", fontsize=9, loc="left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The returner has the hardest decisions on the field, made in the four seconds the ball hangs: catch
it and run, wave for a fair catch, or let it go. A
[**fair catch**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fair-catch) is his insurance policy. While the
ball is in the air he fully extends one arm above his helmet and waves it side to side.[^fc] From
then on, nobody may hit him; the ball is dead where he catches it, and he may not run with it. If he
waves and then doesn't catch it, he still can't be touched while he tries, and he may not block
anyone either.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: the fair catch"}
A returner looking up at a ball falling out of the sky can't protect himself, and a coverage
player arriving at full speed can hit him the instant it lands in his hands. The fair catch trades
his right to advance for his safety. It also makes the punt a strategic choice for the returner:
with coverage in his face he gives up a few yards to avoid a big hit and, more importantly, to
avoid fumbling. The rules also protect him *without* a signal: the kicking team must give any
receiver an unobstructed chance to catch a kick in the air, which is the next rule.
:::

**Kick-catch interference.** A returner trying to catch a punt has the right of way to the ball,
signal or no signal. A kicking-team player who touches him before or as the ball arrives, or gets in
his path, has committed
[**kick-catch interference**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-kick-catch-interference): 15 yards
from the spot of the foul.[^kci] That's why you see gunners pull up a yard or two short of a returner
waiting for a punt, hands out to the side, and pounce only when the ball touches him or the ground.
(A related oddity, covered in
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd):
after a fair catch, the receiving team may try a free fair-catch kick for three points, a
curiosity so rare that Cameron Dicker's 57-yarder for the Chargers in December 2024 was the first one
made since 1976.[^fckick])

**Why returners don't field punts inside the 10.** A punt that lands inside the 10 will often bounce
into the end zone for a touchback at the 20. A returner who catches it at the 7 and gets tackled at
the 12 has *lost* eight yards against letting it go. So returners are taught to stay out of the 10
and let the ball decide, which is exactly what the pooch punt exploits: land it short enough that
it doesn't reach the end zone.

### The punt block

The second choice is to go after the kick. A
[**punt block**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-punt-block) call sends extra rushers, often seven
or eight, usually overloading one side so that the protection runs out of blockers. The rushers'
target is not the punter. They aim at a spot about a yard in front of him, on the side of his kicking
foot, where the ball leaves his foot. Hitting the punter is a foul: running into the kicker costs 5
yards, and roughing him (a harder hit, or contact with his plant leg) costs 15 and an automatic first
down, which turns a failed block into a gift.[^rough] There is no foul, though, if the rusher got a
hand on the ball before the contact, if he was blocked into the punter, or if the punter ran with
the ball out of the pocket without clearly setting himself to kick. That is why a rusher who "whiffs" right at the ball and
then collides with the punter often draws no flag. A blocked punt is one of the biggest swings in
football, because the ball usually ends up deep in the kicking team's territory or in the end zone.
They are rare: about `{python} S["blk_punts"]` a season across the whole NFL in 2021–2025. The reason
is the operation: a 2.0-second snap-to-kick behind a shield leaves very little time, and a block call
costs the return.

Who gets a blocked kick? It depends on which side of the line it ends up. A blocked punt or field
goal that stays behind the line is a loose ball that *either* team may pick up and run with. If the
kicking team recovers it there, it is simply still its down: on fourth down it must carry the ball
past the line to gain, or the other team takes over where it is stopped. If the ball goes beyond the
line, the normal kick rules take over: the receiving team may advance it, the kicking team may not.
(Touching the ball while trying to block it at the line doesn't count as the receiving team touching
the kick.)[^blocked]

### Punt safe

The third choice is defensive. When the punt team might fake (fourth-and-short, around midfield, a
coach with a reputation, a punt team that showed a fake on film), the return team calls
[**punt safe**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-punt-safe): it keeps its regular defenders on the
field or brings them on, covers every eligible receiver man to man, keeps its front at the line to
stop a direct snap, and leaves the returner deep in case the punt comes. Who is eligible on a punt?
The same rules you learned in
[The Twenty-Two](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd): the two ends of the line (here the
gunners) and every player lined up off the line (the two wings, the personal protector and the
punter) may catch a pass; the snapper, guards and tackles may not. That is six men to cover, which is
why the right side of the figure has six dotted lines. Coaches call the linebacker who spies the
punter the "rat" or the "spy." It gives up most of the
return, and in exchange makes sure the punt team doesn't keep the ball. A return team in punt safe
looks like a defense: corners in tight on the gunners, linebackers in the box, nobody turning to set a
wall.

## The rules of the kicked ball

Punts produce more rules questions than any other play, because the ball is loose and both teams
want it. Five rules cover almost everything you'll see.

```{python}
#| label: fig-kick-rules
#| fig-cap: "What happens to a punt, depending on who touches it first. The receiving team can always take the ball; the kicking team can only take it if a receiving player touched it first (a muff) or fumbled it. When a kicking-team player possesses the ball beyond the line, the play is over. Rules from NFL Rule 9 (scrimmage kicks) and Rule 10 (fair catch)."
def box(ax, x, y, w, h, title, body, fc, ec, tfs=8.0, bfs=6.8):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - w / 2, y - h / 2), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=1.2",
                                fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=1.0, zorder=3))
    ax.text(x, y + h / 2 - 2.3, title, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=tfs, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK,
            zorder=4)
    ax.text(x, y + h / 2 - 6.0, body, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=bfs, color=style.INK_2, zorder=4,
            linespacing=1.2)


def arrow(ax, p0, p1):
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(p0, p1, arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0,
                                 shrinkA=2, shrinkB=2, zorder=2))


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5.1))
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 80); ax.set_axis_off(); ax.grid(False)
REC, KIC, NEU = style.DEFENSE_TINT, style.OFFENSE_TINT, "#efeee9"
box(ax, 50, 73.5, 40, 10, "The punt is in the air", "who touches it first, beyond the line?", NEU, style.BASELINE)
box(ax, 17, 50, 30, 22, "Nobody", "into the end zone: touchback\n(ball at the 20)\nout of bounds: their ball there\ncomes to rest: their ball there",
    NEU, style.BASELINE)
box(ax, 50, 50, 30, 22, "The receiving team", "catch after a fair-catch signal:\ndead there, no return\ncatch without one: return it\nnobody may interfere", REC,
    style.DEFENSE)
box(ax, 83, 50, 30, 22, "The kicking team", "first touching: a violation,\nnot a foul. Loose, it stays live;\nreceivers may take it at the\nspot of first touching", KIC,
    style.OFFENSE)
box(ax, 21, 16, 29, 22, "Muff", "touched, never possessed\n(off a hand, a leg, a helmet).\nEither team may recover;\nkickers may not advance it", REC, style.DEFENSE)
box(ax, 52, 16, 29, 22, "Fumble", "caught, then dropped.\nEither team may recover\nand advance it, like any\nother fumble", REC, style.DEFENSE)
box(ax, 83, 16, 29, 22, "Downed", "a kicking-team player catches\nor falls on it first. Possession\nkills the ball: dead there,\nreceivers' ball at that spot", KIC, style.OFFENSE)
for x in (17, 50, 83):
    arrow(ax, (50 + (x - 50) * 0.25, 68.4), (x, 61.2))
arrow(ax, (44, 38.8), (27, 27.2))
arrow(ax, (51, 38.8), (52, 27.2))
arrow(ax, (83, 38.8), (83, 27.2))
h = [Patch(fc=REC, ec=style.DEFENSE, label="receiving team touched it"),
     Patch(fc=KIC, ec=style.OFFENSE, label="kicking team touched it"),
     Patch(fc=NEU, ec=style.BASELINE, label="nobody")]
ax.legend(handles=h, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.03), ncol=3, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

1. **Out of bounds or at rest.** A punt that goes out of bounds is dead where it crossed the
   sideline, and it's the receiving team's ball there. One that rolls to a stop with nobody trying to
   pick it up is the receiving team's ball where it stopped.
2. **The end zone.** A punt that touches the ground in the end zone, or touches a kicking-team
   player who is standing on or behind the goal line, is a touchback: ball at the 20. That's why you
   see a gunner leap from the field, bat a bouncing ball back out of the end zone while he's still in
   the air, and only then land: as long as he hasn't touched the goal line or the end zone before he
   touches the ball, the ball is still alive and can be downed short of the goal line.[^downing]
3. **First touching.** A kicking-team player may not be the first to touch a punt beyond the line.
   If he does, it is [**first touching**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-first-touching), which is a
   *violation*, not a foul: no yardage, the ball stays live, and the receiving team may take the ball
   at the spot of first touching or at the end of the play, whichever it prefers.[^ft] The ball stays
   live only while nobody holds it, though. The moment a kicking-team player *possesses* the punt
   beyond the line (catches it or falls on it), the ball is dead, and if no receiver had touched it
   first, it's the receiving team's ball right there.[^kpossess] That is what "downing" a punt is:
   first touching that ends in possession. The gunner catches the bouncing ball at the 4, play stops,
   and the receiving team takes the 4. The rule also gives the returner a cushion: once a coverage
   man has touched the ball, a returner can scoop it up and try to run, and if he is tackled behind
   the spot of first touching, his team still takes that spot. It isn't a completely free play: the
   option is wiped out if possession changes, so a returner who then fumbles to the kicking team can
   lose the ball.
4. **Muff versus fumble.** A [**muff**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-muff) is touching a loose
   ball without ever possessing it: the punt bounces off a returner's hands, or off the leg of a
   blocker running past. A muffed punt is a live ball, and the kicking team may recover it, but it
   may not advance it: the ball is dead at the spot of the recovery, and the kicking team has a fresh
   first down there.[^muff] A **fumble** is different: the returner caught the ball, possessed it, and
   then lost it. Then it's an ordinary loose ball and either team may recover *and run with it*. The
   NFL sees around `{python} S["muffs"]` muffed punts a season, and when the kicking team recovers
   one the momentum swing is enormous.
5. **The receiving team's own players.** A punt that touches *any* receiving-team player has been
   touched by the receiving team, even if he never meant to touch it. That is why returners shout a
   code word ("Peter!" is the classic) to warn teammates to get away from a ball they're letting go:
   a punt that clips a blocker's calf is a muff, and the coverage team can fall on it.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, a punt that you don't catch is just a bouncing ball that eventually stops. In real
life a loose punt sets off a chain of rules about who touched it first, and the returner is making a
risk calculation on every kick: fielding the ball gains yards on average, but a muff turns a routine
possession change into a turnover deep in his own territory. That's why returners who look timid
on TV ("Why didn't he catch it?") are often making the right call.
:::

## Fakes: why they work, and why they're rare

The kicking team has one more option: don't kick. A
[**fake punt / fake field goal**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fake-punt-fake-field-goal) lines
up as if to kick and runs or passes instead. The common versions: a direct snap to the personal
protector, who runs through a gap; a punter's pass to a gunner or wing who sneaks into the open while
everybody watches the returner; and, on field goals, the holder standing up to throw or run, since
he already has his hands on the ball.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fake
#| fig-cap: "A classic fake punt on fourth-and-1: the direct snap goes to the personal protector (PP), not the punter, and he runs through the middle of the line. It works against a return team that has committed to a return: two of the front players have already turned to run back for the wall (orange arrows), and the vices are busy with the gunners. Against a punt-safe look with defenders holding the line, the same play runs into a wall."
fk = Play(spread_punt(), [q for q in return_team(gw=19.5) if q.key != "PR"], los=50, to_go=None)
fk.highlight("PP", color=PURPLE)
fk.path("F2", [(1.0, -1.2), (9.0, -6.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.0)
fk.path("F3", [(1.0, 1.2), (9.0, 6.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.0)
fk.block("LS", pts=[(0.6, -0.4)])
fk.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, 0.4)])
fk.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.2)])
fk.block("LT", pts=[(0.6, 0.3)])
fk.block("RT", pts=[(0.6, -0.3)])
fk.run("PP", [(-4.0, 0.9), (1.5, 0.9), (7.0, 0.7)], absolute=True)
fld = fk.draw(window=(-16.5, 13.0), lateral=(-23.0, 23.0), title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
ball_arrow(fld, fk, (0.0, 0.0), (-5.8, 0.9), lw=1.0)
say(fld, fk, -6.6, 5.3, "direct snap\nto the PP", color=OC)
say(fld, fk, 10.5, -10.0, "two of the front six\nturning to set the wall", color=DC)
say(fld, fk, -14.5, 4.6, "punter (decoy)", color=OC)
say(fld, fk, 4.0, -18.0, "vices on gunner", color=DC, fs=6.2)
say(fld, fk, 4.0, 18.0, "vices on gunner", color=DC, fs=6.2)
plt.show()
```

Here's the puzzle. In 2016–2025 the play-by-play tags about `{python} S["fp_yr"]` fake punts a season
across the whole league, `{python} S["fp_rate"]` of punt-formation snaps, and they picked up a first
down `{python} S["fp_conv"]` of the time.[^fakes] Fake field goals have nearly disappeared: about
`{python} S["ff_yr"]` a season tagged in 2016–2025, against about `{python} S["ff_9905"]` a season
in 1999–2005. If fake punts convert more than half the time, why don't coaches call them more?

1. **They work *because* they are rare.** The conversion rate is high because coaches choose the
   moment: a look they scouted, a return team turned to set its wall, a short distance. Call fakes
   every week and return teams play punt safe every week, and the rate collapses. This is game theory
   in its plainest form: the right number of fakes is small but not zero, so that the other side has
   to respect the possibility.
2. **The downside is lopsided.** A punt from your own 35 gives the opponent the ball somewhere around
   its own 25, while a failed fake gives it the ball at your 35, 40 yards closer, often with momentum
   and a home crowd behind it. A coach can survive a punt; he gets second-guessed for a week over a failed fake.
3. **The personnel aren't built for it.** The punt team is backups, linemen and specialists. A
   punter's pass and a personal protector's run are plays the unit practices a few minutes a week.
4. **Analytics took the edge off.** Fourth-down models now tell coaches to *go for it* in the open,
   with the offense on the field, in many of the situations where a fake used to be the only way to
   try. Why risk a trick with backups when you can run your best short-yardage play with starters?

Fakes also reveal the deeper logic of the kicking game. Every punt-team formation is an offensive
formation, with the same eligible receivers as any other: the two ends of the line and everyone
lined up off it. A player wearing a lineman's number (50–79) can still be one of them, but only if he
reports to the referee before the play, who announces it to the defense; that is how a reserve tackle
caught a touchdown in the film room below. And every return team is a defense that has to decide what
it fears. When a punt team lines up, the return team is reading it, and vice versa, just as on any other
down.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Ravens 2012–2024, Justin Tucker and the 66-yard kick"}
For most of his 13 seasons in Baltimore, Justin Tucker was the standard for accuracy: he made
`{python} S["tucker_pct"]` of his `{python} S["tucker_att"]` regular-season field-goal attempts.
His most famous kick came on **September 26, 2021, at Detroit**. Baltimore trailed 17–16 with no
timeouts; a fourth-and-19 completion got the ball to the Lions' 48, and with three seconds left
Tucker tried a 66-yarder, two yards longer than any field goal ever made. It hit the crossbar, bounced
up and over, and Baltimore won 19–17.[^tucker66] **What to notice:** the arithmetic (a snap from the
48 plus 18 yards is 66), the venue (indoors at Ford Field, no wind), and the operation: snapper Nick
Moore and holder Sam Koch had to be perfect for a kicker to swing that hard. Tucker made
`{python} S["tucker24"]` in 2024. Baltimore released him in May 2025, the league suspended him for
ten weeks that summer, and he was still unsigned when the 2026 season began.[^tuckerout]
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Cowboys 2023–2025, Brandon Aubrey and the moving range line"}
Brandon Aubrey took the long way to the NFL: a first-round pick of Toronto FC in the 2017 MLS draft,
then the USFL's Birmingham Stallions, then a contract with Dallas in July 2023. He made the first 35
field-goal attempts of his NFL career, a record, and in 2024 he made 14 field goals of 50 yards or
more (in `{python} S["aub50att_24"]` tries), the most in a season in NFL history.[^aubrey] By the end
of 2025 he had made `{python} S["aub60"]` from 60-plus yards. **What to notice:** how a kicker like
that changes the coach's decisions. In 2023–2025 `{python} S["aub_sh50"]` of Aubrey's attempts came
from 50 yards or more, against `{python} S["lg_sh50_2325"]` for the league as a whole. For Dallas,
field-goal range started near the opponent's 42, so a drive that stalled at midfield still had a
reasonable shot at three points, and fourth-and-long near the 40 became a kick instead of a punt.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Jaguars 2025, Cam Little goes to 68"}
On **November 2, 2025**, at Las Vegas, Jacksonville's second-year kicker Cam Little ended the first
half with a **68-yard field goal**, breaking Tucker's record by two yards (the Jaguars won 30–29 in
overtime). In Week 18 he made a 67-yarder at home against Tennessee, the longest ever kicked in an
open-air stadium.[^little] **What to notice:** the setting of the record (the dome at Allegiant
Stadium, no wind) and the season it came in, the first with teams breaking in their own kicking balls.
Little made `{python} S["little25"]` field-goal tries in 2025; the 60-plus-yard kick, a stunt a
decade ago, had become a planned weapon at the end of a half.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seahawks, NFC Championship (2014 season), the fake that won a conference"}
On **January 18, 2015**, Seattle trailed Green Bay 16–0 in the third quarter of the NFC Championship
Game and lined up for a field goal at the Packers' 19. Holder Jon Ryan, the punter, took the snap,
sprinted to his left, away from the rush, and threw a 19-yard touchdown pass to Garry Gilliam, a
rookie offensive tackle wearing No. 79 who was playing the wing and slipped out of the formation
unnoticed.[^seafake] Seattle went on to win in overtime. **What to notice:** the holder already has
the ball in his hands; a wing is off the line, so he is a back and an eligible receiver, and a
player wearing 79 there must have reported to the referee, a detail a block unit sending everyone
at the kick can easily miss; and nobody stayed home to cover him.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Dolphins and Colts, two direct-snap fake punts"}
The fake punt in this chapter's figure, a direct snap to an up-back running through the middle, is
the bread-and-butter version, and it works when the return team isn't looking for it. In the AFC
Wild Card game at Pittsburgh on **January 8, 2017**, Miami, down 17 in the second quarter, faced
fourth-and-1 at its own 41. The snap went straight to safety Michael Thomas, who ran up the middle for
three yards and a first down.[^miafake] For the opposite lesson, find the Colts' fake punt against
New England on **October 18, 2015**. Most of the punt team shifted to one side; wide receiver Griff
Whalen became the snapper and safety Colt Anderson lined up behind him. The play was meant only to
draw the Patriots offside, but Whalen snapped the ball anyway, and Anderson was dropped for a
one-yard loss (with an illegal-formation flag the Patriots declined). It is remembered as one of the
worst fakes ever run.[^colts] **What to notice:** a fake needs surprise *and* a sound formation; the
Dolphins had both, the Colts had neither.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the range finder"}
**On every fourth down, call it before the offense lines up: go, punt or kick.**

- **Do the arithmetic.** Line of scrimmage plus 18 is the kick. Under 40 yards: a kick is nearly
  automatic. 50–55: depends on the kicker and the day. Beyond 58: only for a special leg, a roof or
  thin air, or the end of a half.
- **Check the conditions.** Roof open or closed? Flags on the uprights (and which way they blow
  for *this* end)? A cold night? Did the broadcast show the kicker's warmup line?
- **Read the distance and the score.** Fourth-and-1 at the opponent's 38 is a go in most modern
  playbooks; fourth-and-8 at the same spot is a kick for a good kicker, a punt for a shaky one.
- **When the punt team trots out, look at the return team.** Two vices on each gunner and a
  deep returner: a return. Seven or eight on the line, crowding one side: a block. Defenders on the
  field, corners in tight on the gunners, no one turning back: punt safe, they fear a fake.
- **Watch where the punter aims.** From midfield, a high pooch toward the 10 and gunners racing to
  the spot. From deep, a directional kick to the numbers.
- **Then watch the returner's hands.** One arm waving above the helmet is a fair catch. A
  returner backing away from a ball inside his 10 is letting it go for a touchback. Listen for the
  officials sorting out who touched it first.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the cold kick"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-range
#| fig-cap: "Fourth-and-6 at the opponent's 37, early in the fourth quarter, tied. An outdoor stadium in December: 34°F and a 15-mph wind blowing straight into the kicker's face. This kicker's pregame line into the wind was the opponent's 33 (dashed): from that line of scrimmage or closer, he'll kick."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.3))
fld, p = fg_geometry(ax, 37, show_dims=False, range_line=33)
say(fld, p, 0.0, 3.6, "4th & 6\nopp. 37", color=OC, fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, -8.0, 4.6, "spot of\nthe kick", color=OC, fs=6.4)
(wx0, wy0), (wx1, wy1) = fld.xy(108.0, MIDDLE - 7.5), fld.xy(94.0, MIDDLE - 7.5)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(wx0), float(wy0)), (float(wx1), float(wy1)), arrowstyle="simple,head_width=6,head_length=7",
                             mutation_scale=1.3, color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.7, zorder=4))
ax.text(float(wx0 + wx1) / 2, float(wy0) - 2.2, "wind 15 mph, in the kicker's face", ha="center", va="top",
        fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2)
say(fld, p, 7.6, -9.0, "kicker's line\ninto the wind:\nopp. 33", color=style.INK, fs=6.4)
tx, ty = fld.xy(96.0, MIDDLE + 6.5)
ax.text(float(tx), float(ty), "34°F, 15-mph wind in his face", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
        color=style.INK, zorder=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))
plt.show()
```

**How long is the kick, and what should the coach do?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**It's a 55-yarder (37 + 18), four yards beyond this kicker's line into the wind: punt, or go for
it, but don't kick.** The chapter's weather numbers point the same way. In outdoor games colder than
40°F, kickers made `{python} S["c55p"]` of their tries from 55 yards and beyond, and those were the
hand-picked long kicks coaches chose to attempt in the cold; this one is also into a 15-mph wind. The cost of a miss is
the spot of the kick, the opponent's 45, a short field in a tied game.

Between the other two options it's close, and teams differ. NFL offenses converted
`{python} S["c4_6"]` of fourth-and-6 plays in 2016–2025, and a failed try hands the opponent the ball at its own 37. A punt from the 37 is
the pooch scenario from the heatmap: into the wind it won't carry into the end zone, so the punter can
aim high at the 10 and the gunners can down it. A conservative coach punts and plays for field position
in a tied game; an aggressive one goes for it. The kick is the one choice the conditions rule out.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: what is the return team doing?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-block
#| fig-cap: "Fourth-and-9 at the punting team's own 31, second quarter. The punt team is in its usual spread punt. Count the return team: eight men on the line, three to the punt team's left of the snapper and five to its right; one vice on each gunner instead of two; the returner (not shown) about 40 yards deep."
blk = [D(f"B{i}", "DL", 1.0, w) for i, w in enumerate([-4.4, -2.6, -1.0, 1.4, 3.0, 4.6, 6.2, 7.8])]
blk += [D("V1", "CB", 1.0, -18.3, "V"), D("V2", "CB", 1.0, 18.3, "V")]
pb = Play(spread_punt(), blk, los=41, to_go=None)
fld = pb.draw(window=(-16.5, 5.5), lateral=(-23.0, 23.0), title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
say(fld, pb, 3.6, 4.6, "five on this side", color=DC)
say(fld, pb, 3.6, -2.7, "three", color=DC)
say(fld, pb, 3.6, -18.3, "one vice", color=DC, fs=6.2)
say(fld, pb, 3.6, 18.3, "one vice", color=DC, fs=6.2)
say(fld, pb, -14.5, 4.4, "punter", color=OC)
plt.show()
```

**Return, block or safe? And what should the punt team's personal protector do about it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A punt block, overloading the punt team's right side.** The tells: eight on the line instead of the
usual six, five of them on one side, and only one vice per gunner (strictly, a single "jammer"), because the return team needed the
extra bodies up front and doesn't care much about the coverage if it gets a hand on the ball. A team
setting up a return would have two vices on each gunner and players ready to peel back for a wall; a
punt-safe team would have defenders, not rushers, and nobody committing this many players to one side.
(A side note on the rules: the limit of six defenders on one side of the snapper applies only to
field goals and tries, not to punts.[^fgrules6]) Eight on the line is a strong tell, not a guarantee:
return teams sometimes show exactly this overload and then peel back into a return at the snap.

The personal protector's job is exactly this moment. Before the snap he calls out the overload and
slides the protection toward it, so the shield (the wings and the PP himself) and the right-side
blockers take the inside rushers and
the outermost man is left with the longest path. The punter may also take a slightly quicker drop or
angle his kick away from the overload. The trade for the return team: with one vice per gunner, a punt
that gets off cleanly will meet gunners arriving fast, so expect a fair catch. Fourth-and-9 from the 31
isn't a fake situation, so the punt team just punts, quickly.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: the bounce"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-muff
#| fig-cap: "A punt from midfield comes down at the receiving team's 9. The returner has decided to let it go and is backing away, waving his teammates off, but it takes a short hop and strikes the leg of one of his own teammates (V), a vice who is running back toward the play. A gunner (G) falls on the loose ball at the 7."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
fq = Field(ax=ax, orient="horizontal", los=60.0, window=(21.0, 60.0), to_go=None, lateral=(15.0, 38.5))
no_numbers(fq)


def m(x, y, side, label):
    px, py = fq.xy(x, y)
    draw_marker(ax, float(px), float(py), side, label, fq.pts_per_yard())


def t_(x, y, s, color=style.INK_2, fs=6.8):
    px, py = fq.xy(x, y)
    ax.text(float(px), float(py), s, fontsize=fs, color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9, linespacing=1.1,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def flight(x0, y0, x1, y1, rad, lw=1.3):
    (ax0, ay0), (ax1, ay1) = fq.xy(x0, y0), fq.xy(x1, y1)
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(ax0), float(ay0)), (float(ax1), float(ay1)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                 mutation_scale=9, color=style.BALL, lw=lw, ls=(0, (3, 2)),
                                 connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}", zorder=6))


flight(84.0, MIDDLE + 3.0, 100.5, MIDDLE - 0.2, -0.25)
flight(101.3, MIDDLE - 0.8, 102.6, MIDDLE - 2.6, 0.0, lw=1.0)
m(101.0, MIDDLE - 0.4, "ball", "")
m(101.9, MIDDLE + 1.1, "def", "V")
m(106.5, MIDDLE + 4.0, "def", "PR")
m(103.4, MIDDLE - 3.6, "off", "G")
m(98.5, MIDDLE + 3.6, "off", "G")
t_(99.0, MIDDLE - 6.0, "hits V's leg\nat the 9")
t_(106.0, MIDDLE - 7.5, "G falls on it\nat the 7", color=OC)
t_(106.5, MIDDLE + 7.5, "returner lets\nit go", color=DC)
t_(86.0, MIDDLE + 7.5, "punt from midfield\n(flight shortened)", color=style.BALL)
for xx, lab in [(90, "20"), (100, "10"), (105, "5"), (110, "goal line")]:
    px, py = fq.xy(xx, 16.8)
    ax.text(float(px), float(py), lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.MUTED, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

**Whose ball is it, and where?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The kicking team's ball at the 7: first-and-goal.** The ball touched a receiving-team player, so
the receiving team "touched it first," even though it was an accident and even though the returner
never wanted it. That makes it a **muff**: the receivers touched it without possessing it. A muffed
punt is a live ball and the kicking team may recover it. It may not advance it, so the ball is dead
where the gunner fell on it, and the kicking team has a new set of downs there.

That's why the returner should have been shouting his warning word ("Peter!") as soon as he decided to
let the ball go: every teammate near a bouncing punt is a liability. Order matters, too. If the ball
had missed V and the gunner had fallen on it at the 7 untouched by any receiver, the kicking team would
not have kept it: that is first touching (the gunner simply downed it), and it's the *receiving* team's ball at the 7.
And if it had bounced into the end zone without touching anyone, it would have been a touchback at the
20.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Add 18.** A field goal is the line of scrimmage plus about 8 yards to the holder and 10 for the end
  zone. *Field goal range* is a coach's judgment about this kicker today, weighed against going for it
  and punting, and a miss costs the spot of the kick.
- **Kickers are far better than they were**, so range has moved out about five yards in a generation.
  Wind and cold shorten it; altitude and roofs lengthen it. The data understates bad weather's effect,
  because coaches don't try the kicks they expect to miss.
- A field goal is a **1.3-second snap-hold-kick operation** behind a wall that steps inside and must not
  give ground. Block units overload, crash the middle and aim at the block point; the rules ban
  leaping, covering the snapper and more than six rushers on one side.
- The **2015 extra-point change** turned a 99% kick into a roughly 94% one and made the kick and the
  two-point try worth almost the same, so two-point tries doubled and the choice now follows the score.
- A punt is **protect, kick, cover**. The NFL's base is the spread punt, with the wings and personal
  protector forming the shield in front of the punter; only the gunners may release before the kick,
  so two vices on each gunner is the return team's first priority. Judge punts by **net** and by where the opponent starts, not by gross distance.
- The return team chooses before the snap: **return, block or safe**. The rules of the loose ball
  (fair catch, touchback, first touching, muff versus fumble, kick-catch interference) all follow from
  one question: who touched it first? Fake punts succeed more often than not precisely because they are
  rare.

[^fg18]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 1999–2025 regular seasons: field-goal attempts whose recorded `kick_distance` equals `yardline_100` plus 18. Almost all the rest are plus 17 or plus 19.

[^missedfg]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 11, Section 4, Article 2 (missed field goals: the receivers' ball at the spot of the kick, or at the 20 if the spot of the kick was inside the 20).

[^eras]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 1999–2025: all field-goal attempts (made, missed and blocked) by `kick_distance`.

[^gogolak]: Pro Football Daly, "When soccer invaded football," on Pete Gogolak, Hungarian-born, who kicked the first soccer-style field goal in pro football for the AFL's Buffalo Bills on Sept. 13, 1964: https://profootballdaly.com/when-soccer-invaded-football/ ; Cornell Athletics Hall of Fame, Pete Gogolak: https://cornellbigred.com/hof.aspx?hof=414 . Mark Moseley, generally called the last full-time straight-on kicker, retired during the 1986 season (*Sports Illustrated* Vault, "Mark Moseley," 2018: https://vault.si.com/vault/2018/07/02/mark-moseley ).

[^kball]: Minnesota Vikings, "NFL 2025 rule changes" (owners' approval of the K-ball proposal): https://www.vikings.com/news/nfl-2025-rule-changes ; Fox Sports, "NFL kickers are making more 60-yard field goals than ever, and the balls could be part of the reason" (2025), describing the change (60 K-balls delivered to each team before the preseason and prepared like quarterbacks' balls, replacing a 60-minute pregame window with a towel and brush) and the seven teams that proposed it: https://www.foxsports.com/stories/nfl/nfl-kickers-are-making-more-60yard-field-goals-than-ever-and-the-balls-could-be-part-of-the-reason . The 2025 and 2016–2021 counts are a course calculation from nflverse play-by-play.

[^weather]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2010–2025. Indoors = `roof` of "dome" or "closed"; outdoors = "outdoors" or "open". Temperature and wind come from the game-level `temp` and `wind` fields, filled from the `weather` text where those are missing; neither records the wind's direction relative to the kick. The same pattern shows elsewhere. Indoors, kickers made `{python} S["m50_in"]` of their 50-plus-yard tries and outdoors `{python} S["m50_out"]`, while 50-plus kicks were `{python} S["sh50_in"]` of attempts indoors and `{python} S["sh50_out"]` outdoors. From 50–54 yards, outdoor kickers made `{python} S["m5054_calm"]` with 5 mph of wind or less and `{python} S["m5054_windy"]` at 11 mph or more, and 50-plus kicks were `{python} S["sh50_calm"]` of attempts in calm air against `{python} S["sh50_windy"]` in wind. The cold 55-plus figure rests on only `{python} S["c55pn"]` tries.

[^fgreturn]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 11, Section 4, Article 2, Exception (1): when a missed field goal is touched by the receivers beyond the line, "all general rules for a scrimmage kick will apply," so the receivers may advance it (Rule 9, Section 3, Article 3).

[^cromartie]: The play appears in nflverse play-by-play (2007 Week 9, San Diego at Minnesota, Nov. 4, 2007, end of the second quarter: "8-R.Longwell 57 yard field goal is No Good ... 31-A.Cromartie at LAC -9 for 109 yards, TOUCHDOWN. Longest Play in NFL History").

[^records]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, "Jaguars kicker Cam Little sets NFL record with 68-yard field goal vs. Raiders" (Nov. 2025): https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2025/11/jaguars-kicker-cam-little-sets-nfl-record-with-68-yard-field-goal-vs-raiders ; CBS Sports, "Ravens' Justin Tucker stuns Lions with NFL record-setting 66-yard field goal" (Sept. 2021), which notes the previous record, Matt Prater's 64-yarder for Denver in 2013: https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/ravens-justin-tucker-stuns-lions-with-nfl-record-setting-66-yard-field-goal-on-final-play-of-game . ESPN, "What are the longest field goals in NFL history?" (updated Oct. 2026), for the list of 63-yarders (Dempsey 1970, Elam 1998, Janikowski 2011, Akers 2012): https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/40994229 . Prater's kick (Dec. 8, 2013, vs. Tennessee in Denver), Janikowski's (Sept. 12, 2011, at Denver) and Akers's (Sept. 9, 2012, at Green Bay) are also in nflverse play-by-play; Dempsey's came at New Orleans's Tulane Stadium and Elam's at Denver's Mile High Stadium.

[^optime]: Justin Tucker in *Baltimore* magazine (September 2014), "this 1.3-second field-goal operation, from the snap to the hold to the kick": https://www.baltimoremagazine.com/2014/9/5/justin-tucker-renaissance-raven ; Kicking System (2012), giving 1.2–1.35 seconds as the professional range: https://kickingsystem.com/2012/08/15/special-teams-unit-field-goals-operation-times-working-with-the-snapper-and-holder/ . Published snap times are inconsistent; the roughly 0.4-second snap and half-second hold in the list are approximations (a snap at about 35 to 45 mph covers eight yards in 0.4 to 0.5 seconds) and vary by unit.

[^fgrules]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 9, Section 1, Article 3, Item 2 (field goal or try-kick formation): a defender within one yard of the line must have his entire body outside the snapper's shoulder pads; no more than six defenders on the line on either side of the snapper; no pushing teammates into the formation (15 yards).

[^ice]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 4, Section 5, Article 1, Items 3 and 4 (a second charged timeout in the same dead-ball period is prohibited; an attempt by the defense to call one to "freeze" a kicker before a field goal or try is ignored and is unsportsmanlike conduct) and Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1(v).

[^snapper]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 12, Section 2, Article 9(a)(11) (the player who snaps during any scrimmage kick is a defenseless player until he has had an opportunity to defend himself or moves downfield) and Rule 9, Section 1, Article 3 (on punt, field-goal and try formations, a defender within one yard of the line must have his entire body outside the snapper's shoulder pads).

[^fgrules6]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 9, Section 1, Article 3: Item 1 (punt formation) requires only that defenders within a yard of the line stay outside the snapper's shoulder pads; the six-per-side limit is in Item 2, which covers field-goal and try formations.

[^leap]: Seattle Seahawks, "NFL prohibits leaping block, announces other rule changes for 2017": https://seahawks.com/news/nfl-prohibits-leaping-block-announces-other-rule-changes-for-2017-184783 ; ESPN on the safety concerns behind the ban (2017): https://africa.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/19021659/nfl-expected-pass-rule-prohibiting-leaper-block-attempts-field-goals-extra-point-attempts . Current text: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1(r).

[^tee]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 11, Section 3, Article 2(a): "An artificial or manufactured tee shall not be permitted to assist in the execution of a Try kick"; field goals follow the same rule (Rule 11, Section 4).

[^pat2015]: CBS Boston, "NFL votes to move extra-point kick attempts to 15-yard line" (May 19, 2015), on the 30–2 vote (Washington and Oakland against), the 2014 preseason experiment, and the defensive return of a failed try for two points: https://www.cbsnews.com/boston/news/nfl-votes-to-move-extra-point-kick-attempts-to-15-yard-line/ ; current rule: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 11, Section 3, Article 1 (the ball spotted 15 yards from the goal line for a try kick, two yards for a run or pass).

[^patcalc]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons: rows with an `extra_point_result` (kicks) or a two-point attempt with a `two_point_conv_result`. Team totals are 2015–2025.

[^puntops]: Scouting Academy, "ITP Glossary: Punt" and "ITP Glossary: Long Snapper" (snap-to-kick target about 2.0 seconds, snap to the punter's hands about 0.7 seconds, NFL hang times of 4.5–5.0 seconds): https://scoutingacademy.com/itp-glossary-punt/ ; https://scoutingacademy.com/itp-glossary-long-snapper/

[^guy]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, Ray Guy biography (Raiders 1973–86; the first punter enshrined, Class of 2014): https://www.profootballhof.com/players/ray-guy/

[^release]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 9, Section 1, Article 2: "only the end men (eligible receivers) on each side of the line of scrimmage at the time of the snap, or an eligible receiver who is aligned or in motion behind the line and is more than one yard outside the end man on either side, are permitted to advance more than one yard beyond the line before the ball is kicked." Penalty: five yards.

[^punt74]: *Sports Illustrated*, "The offense is now in command" (Dec. 16, 1974), on the 1974 rule and how coaches found that with nobody released, coverage arrived 12 or 13 yards from the returner, leading the owners to free the wide men on each end: https://vault.si.com/vault/1974/12/16/the-offense-is-now-in-command

[^vicecontact]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 8, Section 4, Article 7 ("If a team presents a punt formation, defensive acts that normally constitute illegal contact ... are permitted, provided that the acts do not constitute defensive holding") and Rule 8, Section 5, Article 3(f) (before the kick, contact that would normally be pass interference against the end man on the line, or a receiver aligned more than a yard outside him, is permitted).

[^oob]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 9, Section 1, Article 5 (a kicking-team player who voluntarily goes out of bounds to avoid a block: five yards) and Rule 9, Section 2, Article 3 (a kicking-team player who has been out of bounds, for any reason, may not be the first to touch the kick beyond the line until another player has touched it; illegal touching, five yards). [^oobpunt]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 9, Section 4, Article 4 (a scrimmage kick out of bounds between the goal lines is the receivers' ball at the dead-ball spot).

[^aussie]: ESPN, "Why the AFL-NFL punting production line stopped," on Darren Bennett, the Chargers' punter from 1995, as the first of the Australian rules converts: https://www.espn.com/afl/story/_/id/20347293/why-afl-nfl-punting-production-line-stopped ; *Sports Illustrated*, "Mitch Wishnowsky and Utah are setting the pace in a new phase of the Australian punter pipeline" (Aug. 2018), on ProKick Australia, founded by Nathan Chapman and John Smith (sources give 2007 or 2008): https://www.si.com/college/2018/08/16/mitch-wishnowsky-utah-australian-punters-prokick

[^puntcalc]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 1999–2025: gross = mean `kick_distance`; net = (`kick_distance` − `return_yards` − 20 × `touchback`) per punt, with blocked punts counted as zero yards; fair-catch share from `punt_fair_catch`. For a touchback the play-by-play records `kick_distance` to the goal line (true of all 156 punt touchbacks in 2025). The heatmap uses `yardline_100` − `kick_distance` as the spot where the kick ended.

[^fc]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 10, Section 2: a fair-catch signal is valid if made "while the kick is in flight by a player who fully extends one arm above his helmet and waves it from side to side"; after a fair catch the ball is dead, and a player who signals may not block until the ball touches a player. An invalid signal costs five yards from the spot of the signal.

[^kci]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 10, Section 1, Article 1: kicking-team players may not interfere with a receiver attempting to catch an airborne kick, or obstruct his path to it, "regardless of whether any signal was given." Penalty for kick-catch interference: 15 yards from the spot of the foul.

[^fckick]: ESPN, "Obscure rule leads to Chargers making NFL's first fair catch kick since 1976" (Dec. 19, 2024): Dicker's 57-yarder against Denver, the first made since Ray Wersching's 45-yarder on Nov. 21, 1976: https://africa.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/43068684/obscure-rule-leads-chargers-making-nfl-first-fair-catch-kick-1976

[^rough]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 12, Section 2, Article 12: roughing the kicker (15 yards and an automatic first down) and running into the kicker (five yards, no automatic first down). The article's exceptions include contact that comes after the defender has touched the kick, contact caused by a defender being pushed or blocked into the kicker, and contact when the kicker carries the ball outside the pocket area without clearly establishing a kicking posture.

[^downing]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 9, Section 4, Article 1(a) (a punt that touches the ground on or behind the goal line, or a kicking-team player touching the ground there, is a touchback) and Rule 9, Section 2, Article 2, Note 4 (when a kicking-team player touches the ball in the air above or beyond the goal line before it touches the ground there, the spot of first touching is where he left the field of play, but never inside the one-yard line).

[^ft]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 9, Section 2, Article 2 ("first touching" is a violation; the receivers may take the ball at the spot of first touching or where the ball is dead; the option is disregarded if the receivers commit a foul that is enforced or there is a change of possession).

[^kpossess]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 9, Section 3, Article 2 ("When the kickers catch or recover a kick beyond the line of scrimmage, the ball is dead at the spot of recovery"; Item 2: if no receiver had touched it beyond the line, it is first-and-10 for the receivers at that spot) and Rule 7, Section 2, Article 1(j).

[^blocked]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 9, Section 3, Article 1 (a scrimmage kick caught or recovered by the kicking team behind the line may be advanced, and if the receivers have not touched it beyond the line the existing series of downs continues), Article 3 (the receivers may advance any kick they catch or recover) and Section 2, Article 2, Note 2 (touching near the line in an attempt to block the kick is not touching by the receivers).

[^muff]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 3 (a muff is "the touching of a loose ball by a player in an unsuccessful attempt to obtain possession of it") and Rule 9, Section 3, Article 2, Item 1 (if the receiving team touches the kick beyond the line, a recovery by the kicking team is legal, "but the ball is dead," and it is first-and-10 for the kickers; a recovery in the receivers' end zone is a touchdown). The muff count is a course calculation from nflverse play descriptions containing "MUFFS," 2021–2025, and is approximate.

[^fakes]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons: runs and passes whose play description begins "(Punt formation)" or "(Field Goal formation)", excluding aborted snaps. The tag is applied inconsistently across seasons and catches a few broken plays, so treat the counts as approximate; "first down" uses the `first_down` field, which includes first downs by penalty.
